blocks.page: projects/Bank Customer Churn Prediction/Bank Customer Churn Prediction-en.html
blocks.expected_text: Product count has a clear nonlinear association with churn: the rate is 7.6% for customers with two products and 82.7% for those with three. Inactive customers have a rate of 26.9%, compared with 14.3% for active customers. These differences prioritize investigation of product fit and barriers to service use. Age and geography differences provide further leads for needs interviews and regional service reviews. Tree models outperform the linear and distance baselines on test ranking metrics. XGBoost+SMOTE achieves ROC-AUC 0.8706 and AP 0.7215, with random forest also a competitive reference. SHAP identifies age and product count as major contributors to this model's scores. Correct and incorrect examples show how explaining score formation helps identify model limitations. Reducing the threshold from 0.5 to the selection-set cutoff of 0.275 expands the list from 459 to 827 customers, covering 93 additional churn labels while adding 275 false positives. The proposed implementation path matches the list to service capacity, investigates product fit and usage barriers, and then evaluates service proposals.

blocks.page: projects/Bank Customer Churn Prediction/Bank Customer Churn Prediction-en.html
blocks.expected_text: This project addresses three retention decisions: which customer patterns warrant investigation, which methods better distinguish churn labels, and how to choose a candidate list within service capacity. Grouped statistics identify patterns, model comparisons evaluate classification methods, and SHAP explains predictions and mistakes. The resulting proposals cover product-fit reviews, service guidance for inactive customers and segmented needs research.

blocks.page: projects/Bank Customer Churn Prediction/Bank Customer Churn Prediction-en.html
blocks.expected_text: The documented source is the public Kaggle dataset Churn Modeling , 10,000 rows by 14 columns, with no missing values. The target Exited records whether a customer has churned, at a rate of 20.4% (2,037 customers). Row number, customer id, and surname are dropped as identifiers before modeling. The four-to-one class imbalance makes recall and PR-AUC useful complements to accuracy. This project compares SMOTE with class weighting; imbalance alone does not require resampling. Always predicting retention gives 79.6% accuracy while detecting no churners, so accuracy needs to be read alongside minority-class metrics. The saved correlation heatmap shows generally weak pairwise linear correlations among numerical features, with age positively and activity negatively associated with Exited. Pairwise correlations do not rule out collinearity in the encoded design matrix or establish causality.

An early rapid-purchase subgroup accounts for 52.23% of fraud labels. The analysis compares recognition across behaviors and periods, then develops proposals for review prioritization and three-tier handling.

This project examines behavioral patterns in first-order fraud, compares model recognition, and considers how a risk team could allocate review effort and handle orders. The data contain 138,376 transactions and 1,415 fraud labels, with prevalence of 1.02%. All 739 purchases made within one second of signup carry fraud labels. This subgroup represents 52.23% of fraud labels and occurs in early January 2015. Recognition differs sharply across this historical subgroup and the remaining transactions. The fit-pool random diagnostic has AP=0.635206, falling to 0.006314 when the one-second subgroup is excluded. Chronological evaluation tests the scope of these patterns. Forward validation selects weighted LightGBM, with frozen temporal-test AP=0.010121 and ROC-AUC=0.595995. Ordinary SMOTE improves neither CV nor test AP over the no-SMOTE comparator in this experiment. Decision analysis separates ranking from action. The specified cost scenario selects approve-all on selection; none of the 131 test fraud labels is flagged, FP=0 and scenario cost is $6,876. The behavioral findings and decision trade-offs inform a proposal to prioritize human review by score and combine transaction evidence with low/medium/high handling tiers.

The task places a risk decision after a new customer's first order is submitted and before shipment. The risk team needs to find suspicious transactions while limiting friction for legitimate orders. The analysis asks which behavioral subgroups contain fraud, what the imbalance treatments recognize, and how scores could assist review and order handling. Inputs include recorded signup and purchase times, value, account attributes, source, browser, and earlier device/IP transaction events. The binary class field supplies the fraud label. Each row is a recorded user transaction and user IDs are unique; the file cannot establish cross-account identity or genuine first-order eligibility. The experiment uses retrospective chronological evaluation to compare approval and rejection under explicit cost scenarios. Behavioral findings inform proposals for human review and tiered handling.

The transaction data contain 138,376 rows and 11 columns; the IP-range table contains 138,846 rows. The analysis focuses on first orders, with GMT timestamps and amounts in USD. Purchases span January 1 through December 16, 2015; signup dates end on August 18. Fields cover user ID, both timestamps, value, device, source, browser, sex, age, numeric IP and target. There are no missing values, duplicate rows or duplicate user IDs. Values range from $9 to $154 and ages from 18 to 76. Target values are zero and one, timestamps parse successfully, and purchases never precede signup. The original file is not purchase-time sorted; 780 rows belong to tied purchase timestamps. IP mapping first checks that lookup intervals do not overlap. searchsorted finds the greatest lower bound not exceeding each IP, followed by an upper-bound check. There are 20,291 unmapped rows, or 14.66%. Fractional values occur in 138,375 IP records; mapping retains the supplied numeric values, whose encoding provenance is unknown. Lookup results do not verify physical location. Country is descriptive only because lookup vintage is also unknown.

There are 1,415 fraud labels and 136,961 nonfraud labels, for overall prevalence of 1.02%. Approving every record would yield high accuracy, so accuracy does not select models. AP (average precision) measures ranking using precision weighted by recall increments, not trapezoidal PR area. ROC-AUC is auxiliary. All 739 purchases within one second of signup carry fraud labels. They occur from January 1 through January 13, 2015, and account for 52.23% of all fraud labels. None occurs in the forward-validation windows, selection or test. Random splitting distributes this early pattern into both training and validation and can repeatedly recognize the same historical structure. This analysis does not independently identify that mechanism or establish a change in fraud strategy. For review design, an extremely short purchase interval is an evidence-backed investigation cue. Its frequency, fraud prevalence and timing should be tracked together; the strong early association does not establish a permanent rejection rule.

The goal Represent information observable at order submission and avoid treating future transaction volume as prior activity. The feature contract Numeric and calendar features are log1p signup-to-purchase interval, value, age, signup hour, purchase hour, signup weekend and purchase weekend. Device and IP counts include only strictly earlier purchase timestamps, excluding the current row and all simultaneous peers. One-hot vocabularies for sex, source and browser fit within each training fold; unseen categories are ignored. The raw dataframe remains unchanged and features are derived from copies. Repeating feature construction cannot re-encode sex destructively. User ID, raw device/IP identifiers, purchase date, target, country and full-window frequencies are excluded. Earlier unlabeled events during validation and test can update counts for later transactions without model refitting. The cost Counts describe events visible in this sampled file and cannot recover omitted production history. Collection latency and subsequent field revisions lack verification logs. No static-window frequency comparator is added, keeping the three imbalance methods on identical event-time features.

The following implementation proposals draw on the behavioral analysis and model comparison. Scores determine where reviewers look first, while transaction evidence informs individual decisions. Scores are not calibrated fraud probabilities. Human-review queue At submission, log the score, signup-to-purchase interval, prior device/IP activity and existing transaction details. Start by recording a shadow queue without changing order status to check data arrival, score distributions and logging completeness. For a trial, review orders in descending score order within a capacity agreed by the business; order waiting time can break score ties. Display rapid purchasing and unusual sharing as investigation cues, without making either an automatic rejection trigger. Reviewers examine existing order and payment-verification records, account activity and device/IP links, then record a reason for their decision. Scores provide ordering, and verifiable transaction evidence supports case decisions. Shared devices or IPs can also occur in legitimate settings; further checks should address a specific concern. Three-tier order handling Low, medium and high denote proposed handling priorities, not calibrated probability bands. The business would set boundaries using selection-score distributions, actual review capacity and tolerance for false declines. Fixed probability cutoffs are not borrowed, and the current test is not used to tune them. Proposed tier Candidate routing basis Suggested action Outcome records Low risk Relatively low score and no additional verification cue in existing records Continue the existing standard process and retain sampled review Subsequent fraud labels, sample-review findings and order completion Medium risk Score in the review range or a behavioral cue requiring a check Add to the standard human-review queue and examine the order and related activity Review decision, reason, handling time and customer wait High risk Higher score accompanied by a verifiable anomaly Prioritize human review; shipment may be held under existing business authority, with human confirmation before release, further checks or rejection Final action, supporting evidence, cancellations/appeals and subsequent labels Trial records and adjustment Before a trial, agree and version the routing rules, review owner, capacity, waiting-time limits and decision authority. Track review hit rate, fraud coverage, legitimate-order interventions, handling time and order completion by date and behavioral subgroup. Sampled review of the standard flow helps reveal cases missed outside the queue. Record label-confirmation and revision times alongside review outcomes. If queue yield, delays or false declines fall outside the business's acceptable range, reduce the queue or return to the existing process before adjusting from new records. The approve-all experiment remains a result under specified scenario costs, not an automatic-approval instruction. Review savings, detection gains and tier benefits remain to be measured.

The protocol uses raw-preserving transformations, strictly prior counts, chronological validation, matched imbalance comparisons and complete score-boundary decisions. Model choice, threshold selection, frozen test and exploratory diagnosis have separate roles. Pilot preparation can organize three groups of information: label generation, confirmation, observation windows and revisions; first-order definitions, event arrival times and transaction history; and fraud losses, false-decline costs, review costs and capacity. The pilot can track user and device relationships, policy changes and review outcomes, then evaluate the model and workflow in new time windows. No performance interval has been established for the dependence structure and selection process; metrics are disclosed as point estimates. Additional tuning cannot remove limitations that require new data.

The analysis identifies a concentrated historical subgroup: 739 rapid purchases account for 52.23% of fraud labels and occur early in the data. Random-diagnostic AP is 0.635206, compared with 0.006314 after that subgroup is excluded. The aggregate random result therefore does not represent recognition of the remaining fraud cases. Behavioral subgroups and periods should be examined separately in risk analysis. The matched comparison selects weighted LightGBM; ordinary SMOTE shows no AP gain in this experiment. Frozen temporal-test AP is 0.010121, above the window's 0.47% prevalence but still weak. Under the specified costs, the selected approve-all decision catches none of 131 fraud labels among 27,676 test transactions and incurs $6,876 scenario cost. Zero detection describes this operating decision; it neither means that every score is uninformative nor demonstrates effective human review. The proposed application combines scores and behavioral cues to assist human review. Relative scores and verifiable concerns guide low/medium/high handling, with review outcomes, order effects and label revisions recorded over time. The deliverables are behavioral findings, model comparisons, decision trade-offs and a workflow suitable for a trial. Implementation preparation should establish actual review capacity, decision authority, verification records and cost definitions. A trial can then collect new time windows and mature labels before changing tiers or models.

Across 9,004 historical loans, term, grade and utilization reveal risk segmentation. Random Forest captures more defaults, while the term rule flags fewer loans for a similar gross simulated cost reduction. These findings inform a review pilot balancing risk coverage, false flags and cost.

The analysis identifies risk segmentation by loan term, credit grade and revolving utilization, and compares three classifiers with simple approval rules. Random Forest captures more defaults, but false flags weaken its cost advantage. The term rule delivers a similar gross simulated cost result with less complexity. The gap between gross and net reductions also shows that policy choice depends on how errors are priced. All analytical fields for 9,004 completed loans come from one full-data CSV, with originations from August to December 2011. The protocol uses 5,402 fit rows for training and cost calibration, 1,351 selection rows for model and threshold choice, and 2,251 test rows for frozen-policy evaluation. Random Forest minimizes selection gross cost subject to recall of at least 75%, at threshold 0.22. Test ROC-AUC is 0.7252 and AP is 0.3535; recall is 70.45%, below the selection constraint. Gross simulated cost is 23.76% below approve-all, with a conditional 95% bootstrap interval of [16.33%, 30.49%]. Net reduction is 4.68%, without a corresponding interval. The term rule reduces gross cost by 24.01%, so the model does not improve that point estimate. This retrospective evaluation uses an already inspected test set and does not certify future gains or performance on rejected applicants. The proposed next step is to retain simple rules as comparison baselines, pilot model scores for review prioritization, and build a checklist around term, grade and repayment burden. Thresholds should reflect processing capacity and actual costs. Recording risk coverage, false flags and review outcomes would help determine whether added model complexity is worthwhile.

The loan sample contains 9,004 rows and 30 columns, with all analytical fields drawn from the same full-data snapshot. There are 319 missing cells: 316 in employment length and three in utilization. About 16.8% of loans charged off. Fit outcomes alone determine unit costs. Mean unrecovered principal among charged-off loans gives gross FN cost of $9,343.77; mean interest among fully paid loans gives FP opportunity cost of $2,267.79. Wrong-decline loss is a scenario assumption with no observed rejected-loan counterfactual. Crediting interest received from charged-off loans gives net FN cost of $6,632.16. Actual review, funding and operating costs are absent.

In this sample, default rates rise from 7.4% at grade A to 52.9% at grade G; 60-month loans have 32.4% default versus 11.3% for 36-month loans. Verified borrowers show 19.4% versus 14.4% for unverified borrowers. These are group associations. Selective verification of riskier applicants is a possible explanation, not a tested mechanism; the analysis does not estimate effects of changing term or verification status. Credit history is the difference between origination month and earliest-credit month divided by 12, without clipping. All 9,004 date pairs are valid and ordered; median history is 12.75 years. Both raw dates are then excluded from prediction. Eleven removed fields also include ID, funded amounts and repayment outcomes; feature engineering leaves 22 predictors. The 316 missing employment-length values are first encoded as zero, together with employment below one year, without a separate missingness flag. This combines unreported and short employment histories. Missing utilization and derived numeric values are handled inside the pipeline. Capping, median imputation, category encoding, SMOTE and LR scaling fit inside the relevant training fold. State and purpose use TargetEncoder, and home ownership uses one-hot encoding. Encoded inputs do not all retain original units. Role isolation limits preprocessing access to evaluation rows, while actual underwriting-time availability remains independently unverified.

Random Forest flags 996 of 2,251 test loans, or 44.25%: 267 charged-off loans and 729 fully paid loans. It misses 112 defaults. The selection recall constraint is a policy-choice condition, not a test or production guarantee. These counts have no measured review queue, processing capacity, recovery rate or operating cost. Use in an actual review workflow needs separate business validation.

Gross FN cost is $9,343.77, net FN cost is $6,632.16 and FP cost is $2,267.79. Selection under net accounting still chooses 0.22. Test net cost is 4.68% below the corresponding net approve-all baseline. No net-reduction interval is available; the gross interval cannot be reused. Crediting interest already received lowers the unit loss of a missed default while leaving the opportunity cost of flagging a fully paid loan unchanged. Capturing defaults therefore yields less simulated saving, and false flags offset more of that saving. This accounts for the lower net reduction and explains sensitivity to the cost definition. Nine cost-ratio scenarios from 3:1 through 5:1 each freeze their threshold on selection rows and all choose 0.22. This describes the checked grid only, without extrapolation to arbitrary prices or operating conditions.

SHAP shows how features contribute to the selected Random Forest predictions, using 2,251 test loans and 24 transformed features. Mean absolute SHAP ranks term, grade and the grade-term interaction first, followed by income and interest rate. The model therefore relies substantially on term and credit-risk segmentation to distinguish predicted risk. The plots use processed feature values. Capping limits extreme numeric values to bounds learned within training folds, imputation fills missing values, and encoding converts categories into numeric inputs. Readers should distinguish original amounts and ratios from encoded values rather than treating every axis value as an original business unit. The direction of the interest-rate association with model predictions agrees with the higher interest rates observed for charged-off loans in exploratory analysis. This helps explain which risk signals the model uses, but does not imply that lowering interest rates would reduce default. Correlations between feature values and their SHAP values are +0.94 for grade, -0.76 for income, +0.92 for interest rate and +0.78 for the financial-stress index. They establish neither global monotonicity nor effects of changing loan terms.

The analysis identifies risk segmentation by loan term, credit grade and revolving utilization, and compares three classifiers with simple approval rules. Random Forest captures more defaults, but false flags weaken its cost advantage. The term rule delivers a similar gross simulated cost result with less complexity. The gap between gross and net reductions also shows that policy choice depends on how errors are priced. The proposed next step is to retain simple rules as comparison baselines, pilot model scores for review prioritization, and build a checklist around term, grade and repayment burden. Thresholds should reflect processing capacity and actual costs. Recording risk coverage, false flags and review outcomes would help determine whether added model complexity is worthwhile. Retain simple rules as comparison baselines The term rule flags 24.74% of test loans, recalls 48.02% of defaults and reduces gross cost by 24.01%; the model figures are 44.25%, 70.45% and 23.76%. Future comparisons should retain both the term rule and model, recording coverage, flag share and cost on the same data and accounting basis. The rule provides a benchmark for added complexity, rather than a ready-made automatic decline policy. Pilot review ranking within processing capacity Of the 996 test loans flagged by the model, 729 were ultimately fully paid. Turning every flag into a decline would therefore create substantial false-decline burden. A proposed pilot would first set the number of cases staff can process per period, then rank model scores and check documents in batches, retaining human decisions and recording handling time, findings and eventual outcomes. Ranking scores are not established calibrated default probabilities, and the offline decline simulation does not measure human-review gains. Turn risk patterns into a review checklist Segmentation by term, grade and utilization, together with model use of term, grade and financial-stress information, provides leads for document review. The proposed checklist would cover term, grade, revolving utilization, consistency of income, debt and installments, and room to meet repayments. It would organize checks without treating any feature as a cause of default or claiming that the combined screening conditions have been validated. Choose thresholds using actual error costs and capacity First specify false-decline opportunity cost, missed-default loss and per-case review expense, then compare candidate thresholds for coverage and workload within agreed capacity. The historical threshold of 0.22 is a comparison starting point, not an established deployment threshold. A new threshold should be evaluated on independent subsequent data, recording whether improvement over the rule baseline covers the added processing cost. Scope of the conclusions This evaluation uses a historical completed-loan cohort, random splits and offline simulations under specified costs. Further work can test ranking stability in new time windows and align feature timing, employment-history encoding and cost assumptions with the approval workflow.

Pet-ownership signals are extracted from 5.819 million channel comments, weak-supervision models are compared, and comment/user scores are translated into a relevance × candidate-scale framework for channel pilots.

This project analyzes 5,818,979 comments from pet-focused YouTube channels to identify textual evidence of pet ownership and shortlist channels for further evaluation. Verified owner labels are unavailable, so interpretable rules create weak-supervision labels. The models use TF-IDF plus comment, user and creator features; logistic regression, random forest and XGBoost provide the comparison, while SHAP is used to inspect model behavior. Restricted-vocabulary XGBoost reaches 0.1915 rule-label test AP, above logistic regression at 0.1179 and random forest at 0.1110. RF uses a smaller sample, so learner choice alone cannot explain the differences. A separate assistant review of 300 new comments uses 294 decidable labels as the reference, yielding conditional weighted precision of 0.8982 and recall of 0.4045. Behavior analysis finds that 67.1% of users comment once and 85.1% appear under one creator. Channel selection should combine flagged-user share with candidate count, followed by comment review and small pilots; model scores indicate textual evidence, while verified identity, purchase intent and advertising return require other data.
new comments reviewed by the assistant 300 decidable / ambiguous 294 / 6 conditional weighted precision; no interval 0.8982 restricted-model rule-test AP 0.1915

Channel selection motivates this analysis. The corpus contains comments, not purchases, browsing exposure or verified household ownership. Non-owners may also buy pet products; no purchasing distinction is measured here. The analysis identifies pet-ownership signals in comment text to prioritize channel review: among each channel's observed commenters, what share has a maximum within-channel comment score at or above the threshold, and how can that share and the flagged count guide review? The main methodological challenge is the lack of verified owner labels for training and evaluation. The project therefore separates the task into two steps: interpretable rules create weak-supervision labels for comparing models, then a new set of comments that was not used for modeling receives model-assisted review for recognizable ownership evidence. The output supports channel ranking rather than identity verification or conversion prediction. The denominator includes only observed commenters, and flags represent textual signals; this share does not estimate verified pet ownership across the channel's full audience.

The course dataset contains comments from pet-focused YouTube channels in three columns ( creator_name , userid , comment ). Dropping 491 empty comments from 5,819,470 raw rows leaves 5,818,979 rows , 2,536,890 users and 3,858 creators. No user ID is null; 32,040 rows have a null creator name. Comments average 77.3 characters, with a median of 43 and a 95th percentile of 249. The following are descriptive properties of the collected corpus. The collection design may affect them, but its contribution is not identified: 67.1% of users comment exactly once. 85.1% of users appear under a single creator. The top 38 creators hold 66.1% of all comments. The Gini of comments across creators is 0.944 . Figure 1. Lorenz curve and Gini describe the same observed creator-comment distribution, so their agreement provides a calculation cross-check. Independent validation of collection or population coverage is unavailable. This is a creator-comment dump, not a user panel. A panel would record what a user watched; this records what a user happened to say under channels the scrape covered. Any user-level aggregate below therefore describes commenting, which is what the scrape captured. A 200,000-comment script sample gives 93.90% Latin, 2.64% Cyrillic, 1.86% Hangul, 0.14% CJK/Japanese, 0.10% Arabic, 0.08% other and 1.28% without letters. Latin script is not an English-language classifier. TF-IDF uses ASCII letter tokens and English stop words; training and full-corpus scoring do not filter to an English or Latin subset. Language-specific validity is unverified. Figure 2. Script mix on 200,000 sampled comments. Latin script is not English; the remaining 6% is also scored. No language-specific performance validation is supplied.

The goal Produce a training label for 5.8M comments when no owner label exists. The choice Rules train the classifier. Section 6 separates the historical 300-comment conditional P80 analysis from the new 300-comment evaluation at a frozen rule threshold. It does not measure a labeling budget or establish that alternative annotation is infeasible. Three explicit labeling functions make the proxy target inspectable: Function Sign Keys on Examples LF_strong_possessive +1 first-person possession "my dog", "we adopted a kitten", "I'm a dog mom" LF_medium_context +1 weaker ownership context "my vet", "his crate", "when I feed my" LF_negation −1 high-precision non-ownership "I want a dog", "my friend's cat", "don't have a pet" The rule A comment is labeled positive when a positive function fires and negation does not. Nothing is learned at this stage; the label is a regex over text. The result The positive rate is 1.52% (88,420 comments), an imbalance of about 1:65. Coverage is carried almost entirely by the strong rule at 1.466% (85,299 comments); the medium rule fires on 0.301% (17,521) and negation on 0.070% (4,049). Figure 3. Coverage per function and pairwise overlap. The medium rule adds little beyond the strong rule, and negation is deliberately narrow: its whole job is to remove one specific kind of false positive. The standalone care detector is not directly used to construct y_rule, but its words overlap the labeling functions: vet, feed, walk, train, adopt, groom, leash and litter are not independent of rule construction. Retaining care_term_count therefore does not establish leakage-free generalization. The cost Two costs, and both propagate to the end of the report. A rule-negative row can be a non-owner, an owner without a matched phrase, or a negation match. It is not confirmed non-ownership; nor are all negatives known positives. The implemented learner is ordinary rule-label classification, not a fitted positive-unlabeled correction model. Rule recall does not estimate true ownership recall. The second is that the label inherits the rules' blind spots. An owner who never writes a possession phrase is labeled negative, and the model is trained to agree. Section 6 samples exactly that region on purpose.

The model drops explicit rule columns and label-rate aggregates while retaining text length, care-term counts and user/creator behavior. The restricted vocabulary removes 39 specified words; the full vocabulary provides a configuration comparison. Care terms still overlap some rule words, so the vocabulary difference does not isolate the contribution of rule reconstruction. Behavior features remain aggregated over the full corpus, including evaluation covariates. Evaluation is therefore transductive within this corpus and does not certify new-user, future-data or actual ownership performance. TF-IDF and IDF fit within each inner training fold to keep evaluation rows out of vocabulary learning.

User IDs define fit, selection and test roles, excluding all 299 users in the historical rubric sample. The roles contain 775,567, 260,296 and 344,882 comments. Three-fold grouped search retains the ten candidate configurations. Each fold fits its own vectorizer and class weight; rule-label F1 selects parameters. The restricted XGBoost uses 450 trees, depth 8, learning rate 0.15, subsample 0.9, colsample_bytree 0.9 and min_child_weight 1. LR and RF provide references. RF uses a smaller sample, so differences cannot be attributed solely to the learner. Model Test ROC-AUC Test AP LR 0.8588 0.1179 RF 0.8576 0.1110 Restricted XGBoost 0.9034 0.1915 Full-vocabulary XGBoost 0.9634 0.3309 All metrics target rule labels. At roughly 1.5% positive prevalence, AP accompanies ROC-AUC; model ranking is not verified identity ranking. Prior test inspection makes these retrospective results.

Frozen threshold and rule evaluation τ_F1=0.848171115 maximizes rule-label F1 only on the 260,296 selection comments before evaluation on 344,882 test comments. Rule precision is 0.2386, recall 0.3101 and F1 0.2697. Of 6,609 flags, 1,577 have positive rule labels. These values do not measure pet-owner identity accuracy. New 300-comment model-assisted evaluation Eligibility requires users absent from model fitting, threshold selection, rule-label testing and historical review roles, nonempty comments with stripped length of at least five characters, and Latin letters comprising at least 0.9 of alphabetic characters. Five exclusive strata use priority negation, strong match, medium match, care and no signal. The S1-S5 sample counts are 60, 60, 30, 60 and 90. Each stratum uses simple random sampling without replacement, with inclusion probability n_h/N_h and comments as sampling units. Stratum Sample size S1 strong match without negation 60 S2 medium-only match without negation 60 S3 negation 30 S4 care only 60 S5 no signal 90 The assistant assigned textual labels without displayed scores or strata; scoring followed annotation sealing. Subsequent row-by-row review occurred after scoring and was not independent blind annotation. No labels changed: 85 support current or former household pet ownership, 209 lack supporting evidence and six are ambiguous. Actual human validation did not occur. New-sample metric Value Decidable / ambiguous 294 / 6 Weighted decidable coverage 98.90% Flags / true positives among decidable labels 54 / 34 Design-weighted precision 0.8982 Design-weighted recall 0.4045 Design-weighted F1 0.5578 Precision is not the unweighted ratio 34/54. Metrics are weighted ratio point estimates conditional on decidable textual labels within the declared eligible population. There are no confidence intervals, full-corpus inference or precision-at-least-80% guarantees. Conditional evaluation of the historical 300 comments Frozen-model scores give conditional precision 0.8692 and recall 0.2369 on that sample. The user-grouped P80 selection procedure gives pooled precision 0.3881, recall 0.2152 and F1 0.2769. Fold thresholds and infeasible states remain separate; there is no validated single P80 deployment threshold. This sample is not merged with the new 300 comments, and historical intervals are not reused.

The frozen benchmark and full-corpus run store their model, vocabulary, threshold and sample scores separately. The full-corpus run regenerated both model and scoring outputs; its restricted-model scores match the frozen benchmark exactly on the checked test, selection and historical review rows. This consistency supports the calculations used in the report but does not extend label evidence beyond the new sample. The full-corpus model scored 5,818,979 comments. Taking each user's maximum comment score flags 94,817 of 2,536,890 users, or 3.74%, at the frozen F1 threshold. More comments create more opportunities to cross the threshold. Comment precision cannot be converted directly into a count of actual owners. There is no single P80 threshold and therefore no P80 corpus user count. Model-configuration differences and error analysis Under the current rule-label test protocol, restricted XGBoost exceeds LR ROC-AUC by 0.0446 and raises AP from 0.1179 to 0.1915, a relative increase of about 62%. This supports retaining the restricted XGBoost configuration in this protocol, but the gap does not identify how it combines length, care context, user activity and creator structure. Full-vocabulary XGBoost reaches AP 0.3309, above the restricted configuration; the comparison does not isolate contributions from vocabulary, rule reconstruction or other settings. The SHAP results below describe fitted-model behavior without providing a mechanism ablation. In SHAP, word_count and comment_len have the widest effects: longer, more complete narratives are generally more likely to receive high scores. Higher care_term_count also pushes scores upward. The model uses care context and narrative detail alongside animal names. The failure modes are visible as well. Tokens such as tf::que , tf::por and tf::los expose language or register shortcuts; creator-structure features such as c_rank_log and c_is_top38 show that channel popularity participates in ranking. Performance within this corpus does not imply stable performance across languages, channels or time. Candidate ranking with review is a better use than automatic identity classification.

Creator ranking requires at least 1,000 observed commenters and uses each user's maximum comment score within that creator to calculate flag share. The denominator is observed commenters, not the channel's full audience, reach or buyers. The first five candidates show that share and scale are different selection criteria: Channel Users above threshold Observed users Flagged share Zak Georges Dog Training rEvolution 6,574 13,404 49.0% Lennon The Bunny 2,881 6,488 44.4% StormyRabbits 1,821 4,285 42.5% Cole & Marmalade 8,755 31,883 27.5% HammyLux 2,114 8,459 25.0% Zak George combines a high share with substantial scale and is a sensible high-relevance pilot. Cole & Marmalade pairs a 27.5% flagged share with 8,755 users above threshold, the largest count in the table; it becomes more attractive when the objective is candidate reach. Lennon The Bunny and StormyRabbits offer high shares at smaller scale and fit lower-budget, higher-relevance tests. This supports a concrete channel-selection framework: segment channels on flagged share × flagged-user count into high-relevance/high-scale, high-relevance/small-scale and moderate-relevance/high-scale groups, then review comments within each group. Shares and counts set candidate priority; they are not validated advertising outcomes.

Actions available now Use flagged share as channel relevance and flagged-user count as candidate scale; shortlist channels that score well on both or match the campaign objective. Rank comments within each shortlisted channel, review the top k, and record the share that contains clear pet-ownership evidence, called precision@k. Sample middle-score and near-threshold comments separately to inspect boundary cases. Split high-scoring comments into care questions, emotional engagement and general discussion so educational content, brand engagement and product research can use different pilot messages. Begin with a small-budget test or offline list review. Compare review yield, candidate scale and content themes before moving to a live advertising experiment. Next model iteration Compare user-level max , mean , top-k average and comment-count-adjusted aggregation, then measure channel-rank stability. Evaluate by language or character-script stratum and monitor shortcuts carried by tokens such as que , por and los . Refit without creator-popularity features and compare AP, the top-k review pass rate and channel rankings to determine whether the model learns comment content or channel identity. If the objective changes from candidate ranking to probability or automated action, add independent human labels, calibration, confidence intervals and time-based validation. Evaluation scope Evaluation uses pet-ownership language captured by rule labels and assistant-reviewed labels as its reference. The new sample covers the filtered eligible comment population, with 294 decidable labels and a conditional weighted precision point estimate of 0.8982. Behavior features use full-corpus aggregates, and user-level max favors users with more comments. Further evaluation can account for language, comment counts and channel-rank stability to improve candidate discovery and manual review.

The level-40 group had 0.82 pp lower 7-day retention, with no clear improvement in day-1 retention or game rounds. The analysis recommends retaining level 30 and testing specific changes to the waiting and return experience.

The product question is whether moving the progression gate from level 30 to level 40 merits rollout. This analysis uses 90,189 public player records to compare retention, check robustness, and examine game rounds. Seven-day retention was 18.20% in the level-40 group versus 19.02% in the level-30 group: a difference of −0.82 pp, with a 95% interval of [−1.33, −0.31] and p = 0.0016. Holm correction and a 10,000-sample bootstrap support the negative statistical difference. Day-1 retention and game rounds provide no clear evidence of improvement; neither establishes equivalence. The recommendation is to retain level 30 and defer a broad level-40 rollout. Further work can log gate arrival, waiting and return events, then run small experiments on waiting messages, return rewards or waiting duration. Section 7 discusses allocation checks and the design of follow-up experiments.

Installs randomized 90,189 (44,700 control gate_30, 45,489 treatment gate_40) Primary / secondary metric retention_7 (7-day return) / retention_1 (day-1 return) 7-day retention change -0.82 pp (18.20% vs 19.02%), 95% CI [-1.33, -0.31] pp, p = 0.0016 Day-1 retention change -0.59 pp, 95% CI [-1.24, +0.06] pp, p = 0.074, not significant Minimum detectable effect about 0.74 pp at the realized allocation ratio, a roughly 19% 7-day baseline, two-sided alpha 0.05, and 80% power SRM p-value 0.0086, assignment-balance flag carried forward Data source cookie_cats.csv , 90,189 rows, 5 fields, no missing values

Cookie Cats places a gate early in the game: a forced wait that blocks progress until it clears. The gate originally sat at level 30, and this experiment moved it to level 40 for a random half of new installs. Moving the gate may reduce early waiting or change players' motivation to return. These are possible explanations; the available fields compare retention and rounds but do not identify the psychological mechanism. Unit of randomization: a new install, assigned once at install time to control (gate_30) or treatment (gate_40). Primary metric: retention_7 , return 7 days after install. This analysis uses it to assess later return. Revenue is unavailable, so its relationship with monetization cannot be tested. Secondary metric: retention_1 , return on day 1. It describes earlier return and does not substitute for a long-term value measure. Decision rule: two-sided tests at alpha = 0.05. Both improvement and harm matter. This is the convention used for the public-data reanalysis, not evidence of original preregistration.

The public source is Mobile Games A/B Testing - Cookie Cats , with the local copy obtained from a GitHub mirror . Its 90,189 rows and five fields cover player ID, version, rounds over the first 14 days, and day-1 and day-7 retention. Player IDs are unique and there are no missing values. Rounds are heavily right-skewed: the median is 16 and the mean is near 52. The maximum of 49,854 is 16.84 times the next-highest value of 2,961. Retention comparisons therefore retain all players, while rounds receive a separate sensitivity analysis excluding the extreme account. Control and treatment contain 44,700 and 45,489 players. A chi-squared goodness-of-fit test against a 50/50 allocation gives χ² = 6.90 and p = 0.0086; the manual calculation agrees with SciPy. This check identifies unusual group counts. Section 7 explains the follow-up and implications for attribution.

Under the assumption of independent observations, the large success and failure counts in both arms support the normal approximation. A simple Wald difference interval is an alternative approximation, while this analysis uses Newcombe intervals to describe uncertainty in the difference. For each metric, H0 is that both groups share the same true retention rate, tested two-sided with a pooled two-proportion z-statistic. The hand calculation and statsmodels.proportions_ztest agree to six decimal places. That agreement guards against both a formula slip and a library misuse. Alongside the p-value, three quantities describe the size of the effect: the absolute difference with a 95% Newcombe interval, the relative lift, and Cohen's h. The z-test uses a pooled proportion variance under the null hypothesis of equal rates. The Newcombe difference interval is constructed from the separate Wilson intervals for the two arms. These constructions serve hypothesis testing and estimation of the difference respectively. metric control treatment abs. diff 95% CI rel. lift z p Cohen's h retention_1 44.82% 44.23% -0.59 pp [-1.24, +0.06] -1.3% -1.78 0.074 -0.012 retention_7 19.02% 18.20% -0.82 pp [-1.33, -0.31] -4.3% -3.16 0.0016 -0.021 The 7-day retention difference is -0.82 pp, a 4.3% relative decline, with an interval entirely below zero. The day-1 estimate has the same direction (-0.59 pp), but its interval crosses zero: no significant difference was detected, and neither no change nor equivalence was established. Both absolute Cohen's h values are small, around 0.02. Commercial importance depends on install volume and operating metrics, not statistical significance alone. These results support evaluating the full seven-day window: day-1 return alone may miss a difference visible at a later endpoint. They do not locate the onset of attrition or prove that waiting caused players to leave.

The primary/secondary labels and test family organize this reanalysis around the two retention endpoints, retention_1 and retention_7 . Engagement in section 6 is exploratory, considered separately and excluded from this correction; it cannot count as an additional confirmatory success. Two-sided testing covers both improvement and harm, avoiding the omission of one direction in a one-sided test. Testing two metrics creates two chances to cross p < 0.05 by luck. Holm is more conservative than no adjustment and controls family-wise error across these two retention endpoints. The step-down correction leaves both conclusions intact: retention_7 stays significant (adjusted p = 0.0031), and retention_1 stays non-significant (0.074). A percentile bootstrap resamples the observed players within each arm 10,000 times; 99.9% of resampled differences are negative. This is a resampling proportion, not a posterior probability that the true effect is negative. The 95% percentile CI [-1.34, -0.32] pp and the analytic Newcombe interval have the same direction and nearby endpoints, but are not identical after rounding. Resampling avoids directly applying a normal approximation to the difference while retaining assumptions about the observed sample and within-arm sampling. It cannot correct potential assignment bias.

With the realized sample sizes and allocation ratio, a roughly 19% 7-day retention baseline, two-sided alpha = 0.05, and 80% power, the MDE is about 0.74 pp. This is a power calculation under specified conditions, not a hard boundary guaranteeing detection. The observed differences are 0.82 pp for day 7 and 0.59 pp for day 1. Day-1 retention has a different baseline, so the two percentage-point differences cannot be compared directly with the same MDE line. This comparison does not establish a smaller true day-1 effect or identify insufficient power as the cause of non-significance. The plotted curve assumes equal arm sizes; the reported single-point calculation uses the realized allocation ratio. Observed (post-hoc) power is deliberately not reported: it is a deterministic re-expression of the p-value and adds nothing. This MDE uses the realized sample sizes and observed baseline. It is a conditional design calculation, not evidence of advance planning or an explanation for day-1 non-significance. The curve also shows the cost of resolution: halving the detectable effect roughly quadruples the required sample.

sum_gamerounds is the volume metric, heavily right-skewed and carrying the 49,854-round outlier. Because a mean-based test and a rank-based test can disagree here, both are run, and both are re-run with the single extreme account removed. The plotted distributions have similar shapes; treatment has a median of 16 rounds versus 17 for control. The Welch t-test gives p = 0.3759 for all accounts and 0.9495 after excluding the outlier. The account affects both the mean difference and its standard error, but neither test detects a significant difference. Mann-Whitney U gives p = 0.0502 and 0.0509, both above alpha = 0.05. For all accounts, the rank-biserial correlation is -0.0075 and the common-language effect is 0.4962, defined as P(treatment rounds > control rounds) + 0.5 × P(ties). These tests and small observed effects do not establish engagement equivalence or settle its business value. The direction agrees with the retention finding, but the volume evidence is weak; the retention metrics carry the decision. Method comparison and interpretation Comparison Question Finding in this project Decision relevance Two-proportion z-test and Newcombe interval Is the retention difference clear, and how uncertain is its size? The day-7 interval is below zero; the day-1 interval crosses zero Prioritize the day-7 evidence and report more than a p-value Raw p-values and Holm correction Does testing two retention endpoints change the inference? Adjusted day-7 p = 0.0031; day 1 remains non-significant The main finding does not depend on ignoring multiple comparisons Analytic interval and within-arm bootstrap Does another uncertainty estimator preserve the direction? Both day-7 intervals are negative with similar endpoints Supports stability across interval estimators, not independent-data validation Welch and Mann–Whitney U Do mean and rank comparisons support better engagement? Neither is significant at 0.05 No reliable rounds improvement; MWU is not generally a median test Full sample and exclusion sensitivity Does one extreme account affect the inference? Welch p changes from 0.3759 to 0.9495; MWU is more stable Report means, distributions, and sensitivity; do not automatically label an extreme record erroneous This project demonstrates experimental analysis and statistical method selection. The methods compare different quantities, so a smaller p-value does not make a method better. The relevant question is what each method measures and whether its result changes the proposed action.

The project supports prioritizing options and planning a follow-up experiment. These limits identify the questions requiring additional data. Allocation and attribution. SRM p = 0.0086 triggers a 0.01 threshold but not a 0.001 threshold. Unequal counts alone do not prove broken assignment. The larger treatment group also has lower retention, making differential inclusion an explanation to investigate. Original assignment logs and preregistration are unavailable, so causal attribution remains conditional on valid assignment. Holm and bootstrap cannot repair systematic bias. Implementation should include checks of assignment, exposure, and filtering records. Behavioral mechanisms. Without install dates and gate events, the data cannot locate the onset of a difference or determine whether waiting caused players to leave. Different day-1 and day-7 results do not establish when a negative effect began. Segmentation. Pre-experiment business attributes are unavailable. Selecting players by post-assignment rounds can introduce selection bias, so retention comparisons retain original assignment groups and rounds remain exploratory. Business returns. Revenue, ARPU, and LTV are unavailable; player-count conversions illustrate scale only. Proposed changes are candidates for testing rather than features already shown to work.

Retain the level-30 gate and defer a broad rollout of level 40. The level-40 group has lower 7-day retention without clear improvements in day-1 retention or rounds. The next step is to locate behavior around the gate and test specific experience changes; Section 7 states the applicable limits. Action Evidence Implementation Evaluation criterion Retain level 30 Lower day-7 retention in level 40 with no clear engagement benefit Maintain the existing setting and defer broad rollout Revisit gate relocation only with a specific new hypothesis and experiment plan Instrument gate behavior Aggregate retention and rounds cannot locate the point of exit Log install, assignment, first gate arrival, waiting start and end, session end, and return times; distinguish exposure from assignment Distinguish leaving before arrival, leaving during waiting, and returning afterward; check event completeness in both groups Test the waiting experience at small scale Relocation offers no clear benefit and its mechanism remains unresolved Keep gate position fixed and randomly compare one change to messaging, return rewards, or waiting duration Specify the primary metric, acceptable decline, sample size, and stopping rule in advance; use day-7 retention as the proposed primary outcome Complete observation windows Day-1 and day-7 evidence differ Wait until each install cohort has seven days of follow-up; evaluating 14-day rounds requires that full window Use day 1 for early monitoring, without declaring equivalence or ending evaluation because it is non-significant Messaging, rewards, and duration changes are candidates whose effectiveness remains to be tested. Gate events help diagnose the experience; formal retention comparisons should retain original assignment groups rather than select only players who reach the gate. Changes involving purchases also need revenue and payment metrics. Future sample planning should start with the smallest business-relevant difference and the baseline for the chosen metric. The current MDE of about 0.74 pp applies to Section 5's sample and day-7 baseline; it is not an acceptable-loss threshold for a new experiment. The two-proportion z-test treats a sample proportion as approximately normal. That approximation is the central limit theorem at work. A reference array and independent samples of size 50 are drawn from the discrete uniform distribution on 1 to 6. Sample means are approximately normal around 3.5, with a standard deviation within 1% of the reference sigma / sqrt(n). This illustrates a normal approximation for sample means; it does not verify assignment or resolve SRM.

The course analysis uses 18,219 Oakland observations to identify pollutant patterns by road distance and land use. Median NO₂ is 23.8 within 0–50 m of a motorway and 7.5 beyond 1 km, both reported on the course file’s original numerical scale. This relative difference supports road-distance features and distance-stratified sampling. Within the tested candidates and selection procedure, random forest outperforms histogram gradient boosting on tract hold-outs, with pooled NO₂ R² of 0.762083 and 0.730200. Random-forest scores are 0.942353, 0.762083 and 0.576017 for random-point, census-tract and coordinate-region hold-outs. Predicting new regions is therefore harder than filling gaps within the sampled area. Industrial-zone NO₂ MAE is 4.283, compared with 2.219 in residential zones, making industrial errors a priority for diagnosis. The relative prediction map covers 628.74 km, or 36.79% of the centerline network, across 25,746 segments. Across 70 tracts, predicted NO₂ and the respiratory-hazard category have a rank correlation of 0.707. These findings inform a proposed plan to screen investigation candidates using grades and model agreement, inspect industrial errors, and sample uncovered areas.

The project asks three questions: how much predictive information comes from road distances and surrounding context, how well models perform at held-out locations, and how their predictions can be presented as comparable road maps. NO₂, NO and PM₂.₅ are modeled separately using the course dataset. Random-point hold-outs evaluate new points within the sampled area; census-tract hold-outs evaluate unseen tracts; coordinate-region hold-outs test transfer across larger contiguous areas. Evaluation, mapping and error analysis demonstrate a spatial data-analysis workflow.

The supplied course dataset contains 18,286 rows and 17 columns describing pollutants, coordinates, road classes, land-use zones and environmental context. Removing rows with missing zone, wind or temperature leaves 18,222 rows; deduplication retains 18,219 observations across 70 census tracts. NO (nitric oxide) has a long right tail. Large values are retained rather than removed solely for their magnitude, so their influence remains visible in distribution plots and prediction errors. The local OpenStreetMap network contains 22,137 directed edges. A projected centerline union avoids counting reversed and overlapping roads twice, producing 1,709.21 km of roads. The network within 50 m of observation points totals 591.19 km (34.59%), describing the spatial coverage of the observations. Road data come from OpenStreetMap , under ODbL, © OpenStreetMap contributors. Pollutants are analyzed on the original numerical scale of the course file.

Six features measure distance to the nearest motorway, primary road, secondary road, tertiary road, traffic signal and stop sign. A metric projection and sjoin_nearest support the queries. Observations and prediction midpoints share build_features() so the definitions agree. Across 100 sampled points, all six distances match individual geometry calculations, with maximum absolute disagreement of 0.00e+00 m. Road class and zone use one-hot encoding. Distances, wind, temperature and population density remain continuous. Training and prediction matrices share the same column names and order. The nearest OpenStreetMap road class agrees with the file's road_type at 95.3% of observations. For 370 points, the file records secondary roads while the nearest network road is primary. Prediction segments use their centerline class; conflicting classes remain ungraded. This comparison illustrates attribute checks after spatial joins.

Random-point, GEOID-tract and coordinate-region protocols each use five outer folds with five inner folds. Fifteen outer and 75 inner splits trace the same 18,219 rows, excluding outer test rows from parameter choices, ablation and fold refits. Tract and region protocols keep each spatial group entirely in training or testing. Selection searches six RF and four HGB parameter settings using mean inner-fold NO₂ R² on all 18 features, then compares four feature sets using RF pooled inner R². NO₂ choices transfer to other targets; HGB uses the RF-selected feature set. This limits experiment size but does not independently optimize features for HGB or the other targets. Parameter and sequential feature choices are nested, totaling 1,096 real fits including final map selection/fitting. The protocols define different spatial prediction tasks, so their results are reported separately. RF uses 300 trees, max_features=0.3 and min_samples_leaf=5; HGB uses max_iter=300, learning_rate=0.1 and max_leaf_nodes=15. Full-data map fitting is not OOF, and OOF scores are not per-segment accuracy guarantees. HGB predicts a minimum NO value of −4.023089 on the surface, without a nonnegative constraint. A useful follow-up is to compare nonnegative target transformations or constrained models for low-value locations.

Grouping observations by distance to the nearest motorway reveals how pollutant distributions vary with distance. Median NO₂ is 23.8 at 0–50 m, 15.1 at 50–100 m, 13.3 at 250–300 m and 7.5 beyond 1 km. Higher values in nearby groups support including road distance as a candidate predictive feature. The binned comparison preserves the observation distribution, showing both trend and spread. Road classes and surrounding conditions also differ across distance groups, so this comparison describes sample associations and informs stratified sampling.

The surface construction first intersects projected centerline unions with the 300 m polygon-buffer union, then segments and takes midpoints. Buffers use 32 segments per quadrant and overlay tolerance 1e-6 m. HTML and static maps use the same 25,746 clipped geometries, each at most 50 m long. The 300 m limit controls spatial extrapolation. The same six final models predict at each midpoint. Each pollutant's prediction-point quintiles define grades, then the worst grade is retained. A–E rank relative predictions from low to high for road comparisons. Context fields including zone/wind/temp/pop_den/GEOID are borrowed from the nearest observation as a nearest-observation approximation; pop_den is excluded from selected final models. RF grade Length km Share of surface length A 67.070822 10.6675% B 102.663963 16.3286% C 120.732140 19.2023% D 157.425536 25.0384% E 180.844492 28.7631% Lengths sum to 628.74 km. RF/HGB agree exactly on 69.92% and within one grade on 96.44%, over 25,746 prediction points rather than kilometers. This comparison measures grade stability when the model family changes.

Respiratory_HI is treated as the course dataset's respiratory-hazard category for an exploratory comparison with pollutant predictions. It is excluded from the pollutant models. Each census tract contributes one row: its category is the mode across observations, and low, moderate and high are ranked 1, 2 and 3 for a Spearman comparison. The surface follows the course aggregation: take the arithmetic mean of NO₂ prediction points grouped by the tract identifier borrowed from their nearest observation. Across 70 tracts, the rank correlation is 0.707 . The low, moderate and high groups contain 10, 16 and 44 tracts, with median tract mean predictions of 7.547, 10.908 and 14.644 . Using tract means of observed NO₂ gives a rank correlation of 0.839; using tract means of held-out predictions at those observation locations gives 0.823. The consistent ordering demonstrates aggregation, ordinal coding and rank association within the dataset. The surface correlation is lower, and its comparison locations also change from observations to road midpoints. Tract associations use fields within the dataset and tract IDs assigned from the nearest observation. A follow-up comparison can clip roads to actual tract boundaries and evaluate the two spatial aggregation methods.

Error diagnostics use RF NO₂ predictions from tract hold-outs. Residuals are observed minus predicted values: positive means underprediction and negative means overprediction. The overall mean residual is −0.381155, its standard deviation is 4.396357, and MAE is 2.969. Zone Observations Mean residual MAE industrial 1,419 0.022 4.283 mixed 3,485 -0.271 3.954 commercial 3,218 -0.696 3.624 open space 224 -1.982 3.008 residential 9,873 -0.339 2.219 Industrial zones have nearly zero mean residual but the largest MAE, showing how overprediction and underprediction can cancel. Residential zones have lower MAE. Open-space predictions are high on average, though that group contains only 224 observations. The spatial residual display uses a fixed random sample of 5,000 observations. The group table and metrics use all 18,219 points. A useful next step is to inspect high-error industrial roads, comparing road classes, distances and observed-value distributions before adding features or changing the model.

Road distance helps identify spatial pollutant patterns, while model suitability depends on where predictions are needed. Higher median NO₂ near motorways indicates that distance carries prediction-relevant information. Under the tested selection procedure, RF performs better than HGB on tract hold-outs, supporting RF as the main mapping model and HGB as a check on grade stability. The comparison supports this choice without isolating an algorithmic mechanism behind the advantage. RF pooled NO₂ R² falls from 0.942353 for random-point hold-outs to 0.576017 for coordinate-region hold-outs, showing that transfer across regions is harder. Spatial proximity and changing feature distributions are explanations to investigate; their separate contributions have not been quantified. Industrial MAE of 4.283 versus residential MAE of 2.219 identifies where improvement is needed. The near-zero industrial mean residual reflects cancellation between positive and negative errors and cannot replace absolute-error diagnostics. The following plan translates these findings into investigation and model-improvement actions. Action Analytical basis Implementation and intended deliverable Screen roads for investigation RF/HGB give the same grade at 69.92% of prediction points and differ by at most one grade at 96.44%; relative road grades are available Flag roads graded relatively high by both models, then consider observation coverage when ordering visits. Put larger disagreements on a model-review list. Deliver a candidate table with locations, both grades and coverage information. Diagnose industrial errors first Industrial MAE exceeds residential MAE, while mean residuals conceal local errors Rank existing observations by absolute residual and inspect road classes, distances and high values. If feature gaps emerge, assess traffic or industrial-activity information. Deliver hypotheses about errors and targeted feature proposals. Stratify additional sampling Values are higher near motorways, region-hold-out scores fall, and predictions cover only part of the road network Account for motorway distance, land use and existing coverage, prioritizing industrial and uncovered areas. Reserve entire new regions for testing. Deliver proposed sampling locations and a spatial evaluation design. Combine tract information for investigation planning Predicted NO₂ and the respiratory-hazard category have a rank correlation of 0.707 across 70 tracts Flag tracts high on both measures, then consider coverage and error diagnostics. Check nearest-observation assignments against actual tract boundaries before selecting sites. Deliver proposed tract investigation priorities. Examine low predictions and compare remedies HGB produces a minimum NO prediction of −4.023089 Compare nonnegative target transformations or constrained models under the same spatial hold-outs, checking both overall error and low-value bias. Deliver a comparison of the original and revised methods. The project delivers pollutant-pattern analysis, nested model comparisons, error diagnosis and relative road prediction maps. A–E grades, model agreement and tract-level field associations inform proposals for road investigations and additional sampling.

Topic, rating, and trend analyses inform proposed actions for quality review, clearer product information, gift-oriented merchandising tests, and review monitoring. Stack: Python · pandas · scikit-learn · gensim · NLTK · matplotlib.

blocks.source: D:\data projects\amazon user review - Document Clustering and Topic Modeling\Amazon_Watch_Reviews_Report.md
blocks.expected_text: This is an unsupervised read of 960,713 US watch reviews (2001 to 2015) with two complementary models: K-Means on TF-IDF for hard groups, and LDA on word counts for soft, overlapping topics. The recipe is selected on a seeded 50,000-review sample; 858,170 full-corpus reviews pass the length threshold, and 858,037 remain for fitting and scale comparisons after zero-vector removal. On the sample, neither the cosine silhouette nor the elbow selects a cluster count (the silhouette is near 0.01 and inertia has no clear elbow). K*=7 is chosen from interpretable cluster content; T*=10 is the smaller topic count on the coherence plateau, while perplexity does not favor adding topics. Under a large mass of generic praise, three concrete themes recur in both models and line up with a star rating the text models never saw: timekeeping and battery, band and sizing, and gifting. The lowest-rated full-corpus topic provides a review-triage signal: a malfunction/returns topic averages 2.37 stars, roughly 1.4 below the next-lowest topic, and holds 52.9% of modeled one-star reviews. High topic shares occur in LED, silicone, and rhinestone product-title groups; their low-price positioning is unverified. The time trend is sensitive to review-length selection: value praise is nearly flat within long reviews, but this descriptive check cannot rule out changing preferences. Trust the themes over the hard partition: the concrete clusters reproduce at top-term Jaccard 0.60 to 0.67 while the partition itself stays weakly separated, so the report distinguishes sample clusters, full-corpus dominant-topic shares, and mean topic weights rather than treating them as interchangeable. These findings support proposals for functional-issue triage, clearer sizing and operating instructions, gift-oriented merchandising tests, and review-trend monitoring.

blocks.source: D:\data projects\amazon user review - Document Clustering and Topic Modeling\Amazon_Watch_Reviews_Report.md
blocks.expected_text: A seller or category manager looking at a review corpus wants to know what buyers actually write about, so that quality work and merchandising can be aimed at real concerns instead of guesses. Watch reviews make that hard in a specific way: they are short, and about six in ten are five-star, so there is no clean, separable customer segmentation waiting to be found. The useful question is narrower, and it has three parts. What structure does the text actually contain? How much of it is real signal or an artifact of a few high-frequency filler words? And which metadata does that structure line up with: star rating, verified purchase, year of review? Nothing in the data carries a topic label or a segment label; the work is therefore unsupervised throughout. Two models look at the same corpus from different angles, and a structure that both recover is more credible than one that only one of them reports. The data The corpus is the Watches slice of the Amazon Customer Reviews dataset: 15 columns, 960,872 raw records, all marketplace = US and product_category = Watches , spanning April 2001 to August 2015. Dropping the 159 rows with an empty body leaves 960,713 reviews . The review text is in review_body ; star_rating , verified_purchase , review_date , and product_title supply the metadata the analysis crosses the text against. The source is Amazon Customer Reviews; the AWS dataset notice describes the original distribution channel.

blocks.source: D:\data projects\amazon user review - Document Clustering and Topic Modeling\Amazon_Watch_Reviews_Report.md
blocks.expected_text: Four facts about the corpus shape everything downstream. Ratings are J-shaped: 59.5% are five-star, with a secondary bump of 8.9% at one star. 86.5% of reviews are verified purchases. The median body length is 149 characters; the random sample has a median of about 14 content stems after cleaning. And 9.0% of review bodies are exact duplicates, mostly short praise like "Love it", retained under the original-record policy; review authenticity is not independently verified. Figure 1. The distribution is J-shaped: a tall five-star bar, a low middle, and a secondary lift at one star. A mean rating hides this shape, which is why the analysis works with the mix instead of the average. Why the sample has to be random The file is sorted by date descending, which puts the first 1,000 rows on a single day (2015-08-31) instead of a spread across the corpus. A head-of-file slice therefore covers only one day. Method selection uses a seeded random draw of 50,000 reviews, and the plotted star-rating, verified-purchase, and year margins are close to those of the corpus. Figure 2. Star rating, verified share, and year, for the 50,000-review sample against the full population. The three margins track closely. This descriptive check does not establish unbiased joint distributions or topic estimates, or representativeness of all buyers. Interpretation. The structure worth finding is the handful of concrete complaints underneath the praise. A large block of generic five-star text will dominate any unsupervised grouping; the analysis is built to read what sits beneath it.

blocks.expected_text:
The goal Turn raw review text into one matrix both models can read, without paying for tokenization twice or letting the two models see different words. Cleaning and the modeling scope One preprocessing function, reused verbatim in the full-corpus notebook so the two runs are comparable, lowercases each body, strips HTML residue ( 13.7% of sample bodies carry a tag or character entity such as
or " ), keeps alphabetic tokens of at least three letters, drops NLTK English stopwords, and Snowball-stems what remains. A review enters the modeling corpus only if it has at least three content stems ; this is an analysis threshold, not evidence that shorter text contains no information. That scope removes 10.8% of the sample, and what it removes is the shortest, happiest text: the dropped reviews average 4.53 stars against 4.09 for the kept ones. Modeling also removes zero vectors after vocabulary pruning, leaving 44,592 sample reviews; full-corpus results below use their own final-matrix scope. Counts first, TF-IDF derived CountVectorizer(min_df=20, max_df=0.5) fits the vocabulary once, at 2,800 terms . The max_df=0.5 cutoff removes watch itself, a term above the document-frequency threshold, so this analysis does not add a separate domain stopword list. TF-IDF is then derived from that same count matrix with TfidfTransformer(sublinear_tf=True, norm="l2") . Word counts preserve the token-occurrence interpretation of LDA, and the code applies ordinary K-Means to L2-normalized TF-IDF; it has no additional centroid-normalization step and should not be described as spherical K-Means. Fitting counts first and deriving TF-IDF lets both models share one vocabulary, which is what makes their agreement in section 6 meaningful. Interpretation. The two models share a vocabulary. Because the count matrix and the TF-IDF matrix are built from the same terms, shared themes provide internal consistency evidence, but the shared bag-of-words representation also imposes common limits and does not verify topic labels. The cost The three-stem floor trades coverage for signal. It discards 10.8% of reviews, and those reviews are not random: they are disproportionately short five-star praise. The gifting and value themes below are therefore measured on a corpus that excludes some of the shortest, highest-rated reviews.

blocks.expected_text: The goal Split the reviews into hard groups of similar text, and decide how many groups from evidence instead of by decree. Choosing K The sweep runs K from 2 to 15 and looks at two things: inertia (the elbow) and the cosine silhouette on a 10,000-review subsample. Neither gives a clean answer. The silhouette runs from 0.0106 to 0.0164 and generally rises with local fluctuations, without a distinct optimum, and inertia falls by less than 4% across the whole range with no knee. Short, positive review text does not carve into well-separated balls, and K has to be a modeling choice. Figure 3. Inertia (left) bends smoothly with no knee; the silhouette (right) sits near 0.01 and generally rises with small local fluctuations. The scores vary little across the scan and show weak separation; neither curve provides a distinct optimum. K*=7 is chosen for interpretable cluster content; the reading that smaller K merges concrete themes into praise remains exploratory and is not validated against independent labels. Neither metric contradicts the choice, and neither makes it; content settles it. The seven clusters At K=7, four of the clusters (about 53% of the modeled corpus) are generic praise separated by adjective and length instead of subject: a "good"-led cluster, a "great"-led cluster, a "nice"-led cluster, and a long-narrative cluster (30.1%) that touches price, looks, and caveats at once. The other three carry a real subject: timekeeping and battery (22.0%), band and sizing (13.8%), and gifting (11.1%). Those three are what the rest of the analysis tracks. Figure 4. Top terms by centroid weight for each cluster. Clusters 4, 5, and 6 read as band/sizing, gifting, and timekeeping/battery; the rest are praise graded by adjective. Do the clusters mean anything? Clustering used only the text. Crossing the clusters with star rating, which they never saw, is the first test of whether they mean more than shared words. Figure 5. Star-rating mix within each cluster (left) and mean star per cluster (right). Gifting is the happiest cluster at 4.79 stars, timekeeping and battery the least happy at 3.73, with band and sizing below the corpus mean at 3.96. Interpretation. What separates the clusters is subject and sentiment, not a clean geometry. The text-only groups sort themselves by a rating they never saw, from 4.79 stars for gifting down to 3.73 for timekeeping and battery, and that alignment is the first evidence the groups carry meaning beyond word co-occurrence.

Concrete clusters have relatively high top-term overlap; the two concern-cluster shares change (timekeeping 22% to 14%, band/sizing 14% to 19%). Aligned cluster shares also change. This comparison does not track individual review assignments or isolate the contributions of corpus, vocabulary, and algorithm changes, so it cannot attribute the change to borderline reviews switching clusters. The topics realign at a softer mean Jaccard of 0.333 , indicating limited word-content overlap across settings. The algorithm assigns a counterpart to every topic; this does not establish semantic stability. The weakest match (0.14) pairs with the full-corpus malfunction/returns topic, whose high-weight reviews support that label, but it does not establish that 960k reviews improve topic quality over the 50k sample.
