blocks.expected_text: The analysis supports four practical proposals: prioritize functional problems for review, improve product-fit and operating information, test gift-oriented merchandising, and monitor review themes alongside text length. Each proposal sets out its analytical basis, implementation steps and suggested evaluation measures. Method choice: use each model for a specific task K-Means provides groups of similar reviews for exploration, while LDA represents several topics within a review. Both reveal content about timekeeping and batteries, bands and sizing, and gifts, supporting the use of these themes to organize review analysis. Cosine silhouettes near 0.01 indicate weak separation, and sample-to-full topic-word overlap is limited. Short text, repeated praise words, and mixed topics are plausible explanations, although their individual contributions were not tested. An implementation should therefore use topic retrieval with human review instead of treating cluster IDs as stable customer types. The models provide useful leads for organizing content, with insufficient evidence for automatic customer segmentation. Quality review: start with malfunction and return complaints The full-corpus malfunction/returns topic averages 2.37 stars and accounts for 52.9% of modeled one-star reviews. Among product-title groups with at least 300 modeled reviews, the ten highest topic shares range from 24.6% to 39.9%. These findings establish a review order: start with title groups containing concentrated functional complaints, then inspect the individual reviews. A quality or support team could first match these titles to the product catalog and separate watches from tools. Review priorities should consider both topic share and the number of relevant reviews. Reviewers could classify the text into stopped watches, batteries, hands, arrival condition, and return experiences, then use those categories to examine inspection checks, instructions, and support procedures for the relevant products. A pilot could track the proportion of recommended reviews that contain the target problem, review time per useful finding, and agreement with support issue categories. With linked order and return data, a later evaluation could assess whether the response reduces recurring problems. Topic share itself is not a product failure rate. Product information: address fit and operating questions The sample band/sizing cluster averages 3.96 stars and the timekeeping/battery cluster 3.73. Relevant topic terms include wrists, links, buttons, and setting the time. This makes fit and function sensible areas to investigate through product information and operating guidance. A team could inspect these reviews to separate actual malfunction, poor fit, and operating difficulty. For confirmed information gaps, product pages could include supported wrist sizes, strap or link adjustment instructions, clear time-setting steps, and battery-care guidance consistent with the product specifications. A pilot on products receiving relevant inquiries could compare fit and operating inquiry shares, recurring negative-review content, and support handling time before and after the change. The proposal tests whether clearer information helps; it does not assume that instructions resolve every functional complaint. Gift merchandising: test the purchase occasion The sample gifting cluster averages 4.79 stars and contains language about buying for a husband or wife. This identifies a purchase occasion worth exploring alongside personal use. For suitable products, a team could test gift-oriented presentation organized by recipient and occasion, with clear sizing, packaging, and return-policy information. Comparing this presentation with the existing page on clicks, add-to-cart behavior, conversion, and returns would inform whether to expand it. The proposal draws on the association between gifting language and higher ratings. The cluster identifies an occasion for testing, rather than assigning a permanent identity to every buyer. Review monitoring: track themes and text length together Median review length falls from 26 content stems to 10. Among reviews with at least 20 stems, mean value-praise weight changes from 7.0% to 7.1%, without the marked increase seen in the full modeled corpus. Direct year-to-year topic comparisons can therefore incorporate changes in review length. A recurring review dashboard could show topic weights, ratings, review counts, and length distributions together. The complete modeled corpus and long-review subset should appear side by side, with representative reviews available for inspection. A model or vocabulary update should be compared in parallel before extending an existing trend series. A historical review of unusual months could record which alerts persist after length stratification and the proportion judged useful by reviewers. The model would flag changes for investigation, rather than treating topic share as a direct measure of changing preferences. Interpretation. Start with human review of malfunction/return content, then improve product information based on confirmed issues. Test gift merchandising separately and use the review dashboard for ongoing monitoring. The deliverable is a set of identified problems, reasoned method choices, and implementation proposals with evaluation criteria.

blocks.expected_text: This study asks which groups in public loan data face greater default risk and whether prediction models can help allocate limited review capacity. It selects 800,634 loans with elapsed terms and terminal outcomes, examines grouped default rates, effect sizes, binned trends and correlations, then excludes post-origination information and compares logistic regression, random forest and LightGBM using a temporal split. A separate selection set determines the model and threshold; policy costs are evaluated under alternative accounting assumptions. Equal-capacity rule comparisons, paired bootstrap intervals and SHAP explanations assess incremental ranking value and model behavior. Default rates rise from 5.6% for grade A to 39.8% for grade G, while 60-month loans show 25.7% versus 14.4% for 36-month loans. LightGBM achieves the highest test AP, 0.315991. Its flagged group has a 25.17% default rate, approximately 1.60 times the overall test rate. However, the selected threshold flags 44.34% of loans: false positives leave gross simulated costs 7.63% lower but net costs 21.48% higher. At a fixed 10% capacity, LightGBM precision is 37.88%, versus 32.38% for the grade rule, with a 95% difference interval of 4.97–6.08 percentage points. SHAP identifies subgrade, recent account openings and repayment-burden features as major contributors. The resulting recommendation is to prioritize capacity-limited manual review, use grade, term and credit burden to guide checks, and select thresholds against missed defaults, false flags and review costs.

Dimension Full-data analysis Sample comparison or interpretation Loan term Default rates are 25.7% for 60-month loans and 14.4% for 36-month loans, a ratio near 1.8 The smaller sample has a ratio near 2.9; neither comparison identifies the causal effect of extending a term Credit grade Default rates increase from A to G, spanning 5.6%–39.8% The smaller sample spans 7.4%–52.9%, with the same direction and a different magnitude Interest rate and utilization Interest-rate correlation with default is 0.213; utilization correlation is 0.050, with increasing binned default rates The sample interest-rate correlation is 0.265; differences in correlation do not directly establish flatter slopes Income verification Default rates are 11.9% for Not Verified, 15.8% for Source Verified and 18.5% for Verified More frequent verification of higher-risk applicants is an untested explanation; the association does not show that verification increases default risk Time windows, loan composition and processing differ. Changes cannot be attributed solely to sample size or period, nor do they establish independent sources or replicated risk mechanisms.

blocks.expected_text: A default predictor must use information available when a decision is made. This step checks the original 151 columns, excludes subsequent repayment and outcome information, and then handles missing values, categories and engineered features. Using later information is called data leakage: it can inflate offline performance while being unavailable for new-loan predictions. The issue here is the timing of predictive information, not a disclosure of personal data. Missingness and near-constant screening fit within each training fold. Median imputation, encoding, LR scaling, TargetEncoder and class weights follow the same role boundaries, preventing selection/test distributions or labels from entering fitting. The final fit selects 57 candidate fields; each fold determines its own count. Field exclusions limit post-origination information; quality screening does not independently establish approval-time availability. Credit-history, loan-to-income and installment-to-income features use fixed definitions. Class weights address imbalance; this cohort has no SMOTE ablation establishing which approach is better.

blocks.expected_text: A July-2015 boundary holds out later loans, while earlier training is split into fit and selection. Parameters are selected by three-fold average precision on a stratified sample of at most 200,000 fit rows. Logistic regression, random forest and LightGBM compare linear and tree-based approaches. Selection chooses model and threshold under the recall constraint, without merging selection into a refit. The separate selection role reduces final training size; stratified inner folds are not forward-chaining validation. The previously inspected test supports conditional retrospective evaluation. Model Frozen threshold Test ROC-AUC Test AP Recall Logistic 0.44 0.705346 0.299581 70.85% Random Forest 0.43 0.709180 0.304748 69.25% LightGBM 0.46 0.717803 0.315991 70.90% AP means average precision. Test point estimates establish neither significant model differences nor deployment readiness. LightGBM improves test AP by approximately 0.0164 over Logistic and 0.0112 over Random Forest. Recall is similar across the three models, so the visible advantage is ranking quality rather than substantially greater coverage at the selected thresholds. Trees can represent nonlinearities and interactions, a plausible methodological explanation, Section 7 uses SHAP to explain model outputs, while the source of ranking gains remains untested by ablation. LightGBM is a candidate ranking model, with Logistic retained to compare ranking benefits against maintenance costs. Rules and models at equal review capacity The primary comparison fixes review volume at 10% of each batch, with 5% and 20% capacity references. Candidate rules rank by worse grade, lower FICO or higher DTI; selection precision at 10% chooses the grade rule. A fixed, label-independent hash ordering breaks ties. Logistic and LightGBM use frozen model scores. Every method flags the same number of loans in the same test set, comparing detection at equal workload. Method Flagged loans Defaults found Precision Recall Net simulated cost reduction Grade rule 27,147 8,790 32.38% 20.57% 1.74% Logistic 27,147 9,813 36.15% 22.96% 5.18% LightGBM 27,147 10,282 37.88% 24.06% 6.76% Within the same 27,147-loan queue, LightGBM identifies 1,492 more defaults than the grade rule and 469 more than Logistic. It has higher precision and net simulated cost reduction at all three evaluated capacities, supporting it as a review-ranking candidate. At 10% capacity, roughly 76% of defaults remain outside the queue: this is a resource-constrained prioritization policy, not a high-recall policy. Fixed-volume ranking produces a threshold that varies with each batch's score distribution. It differs from the main fixed 0.46 threshold and its high-recall objective. The 10% capacity was specified before evaluation, not optimized on test outcomes. Simulated costs use fit-derived average prices to compare policies at fixed capacity. Paired bootstrap: conditional uncertainty in differences Labels and the three methods' fixed flags for the same loans are jointly resampled 2,000 times. The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of each difference form a 95% interval. Multinomial sampling over joint label-and-flag categories is exactly equivalent to paired row resampling for these count-based metrics and preserves correspondence across methods. LightGBM versus Precision difference (pp) 95% interval Net cost reduction difference (pp) 95% interval Grade rule 5.50 4.97–6.08 5.02 4.55–5.56 Logistic 1.73 1.34–2.14 1.58 1.23–1.95 At the primary capacity, these intervals lie above zero, supporting LightGBM's advantage in this fixed-prediction comparison. Intervals assume IID loans and condition on models, prices, rule selection and original queue membership. Each replicate neither reranks loans nor retrains models; tuning uncertainty and temporal dependence are excluded, and multiple intervals are not adjusted for simultaneous inference.

blocks.expected_text: The model concentrates higher-risk loans. The test set contains 271,471 loans, of which 42,739 defaulted. The overall default rate is 15.74% . The model flags 120,374 loans, including 30,304 defaults. The flagged group has a 25.17% default rate, approximately 1.60 times the overall rate. This supports review prioritization, although roughly three quarters of flagged loans ultimately repaid normally. False flags explain the policy cost. Each detected default comes with approximately 2.97 normally repaid loans falsely flagged . Under the fixed-price model, improvement relative to approving all loans is: Cost improvement = Correctly flagged defaults × Avoided cost per default − False flags × Cost per false flag Under gross prices, each detected default can offset approximately 3.33 false flags; under net prices, only 2.28. The observed ratio of 2.97 lies between them, explaining why the same policy helps under gross accounting and hurts under net accounting. This explains the simulation; it does not assume manual review can actually prevent every associated loss. Thresholds must reflect the objective. A threshold of 0.46 offers greater coverage and workload. The frozen net-cost scenario without a recall floor uses 0.70, flags 5.64%, and recalls only 14.87%. These scenarios show trade-offs, not a future optimal threshold selected from test performance. SHAP: how the model forms its predictions The frozen LightGBM is explained using 128 fit loans as background and 1,024 test loans chosen by fixed hash ordering. TreeExplainer uses interventional feature perturbation and raw log-odds output. Home-ownership one-hot contributions are summed per loan before mean absolute aggregation. The maximum difference between reconstructed and model raw outputs is 1.25×10⁻⁷, passing the additivity check. Scores are not probability-calibrated. The largest mean absolute contributions come from subgrade, accounts opened in the past 24 months, DTI, loan-to-income and home ownership. The model therefore uses recent credit expansion and repayment-burden information alongside existing credit ratings. SHAP explains score construction; separate predictive gains from each input would still require ablation. Four cases use the existing 0.46 threshold to define TP, FP, FN and TN. Within the fixed explanation sample, each case is the loan closest to its group's median score, avoiding a selection of only narratively convenient extremes. Red contributions raise raw output and blue contributions lower it. Units are log-odds, not default-probability percentage points. Correctly flagged default (TP, score 0.617): DTI, subgrade and FICO raise the score, partially offset by other inputs. Falsely flagged repaid loan (FP, score 0.565): subgrade, months since the most recent bankcard account and FICO raise the score, but the loan ultimately repaid normally. Risk attributes do not determine individual outcomes. Missed default (FN, score 0.386): recent account openings and months since the most recent bankcard account contribute negatively; positive contributions do not lift the score above the threshold. Correctly unflagged repaid loan (TN, score 0.292): recent openings, loan-to-income, subgrade and DTI contribute to a lower score. Correlated inputs such as grade and subgrade may share attribution; target encoding also affects interpretation. Every temporal test loan has a 36-month term, but the background contains other terms, so term can still contribute relative to that background. This does not mean term differentiates loans within the test window. Attribution explains the model rather than causal effects or automatic rejection reasons.

blocks.expected_text: Finding Proposed implementation What to observe next Grade, term and credit burden show risk differences; employment-length differences are narrower Display grade, term, DTI, utilization, FICO and recent account openings in review; check repayment burden and credit expansion without treating any single field as an automatic rejection rule Review hit rates, group sizes and normally repaid loans flagged E–G represent 6.7% of loans and 14.1% of default counts Monitor higher-risk grades closely and rank within groups using model scores; retain checks in other grades to avoid missing defaults elsewhere Default-count contribution, coverage and review volume by group The flagged group has approximately 1.60 times overall risk, but 0.46 flags 44.34% Start with shadow scoring or assisted manual review; size the queue to daily capacity and record reviewer outcomes, keeping flags distinct from rejection Hit rate at fixed volume, handling time and effects on normally repaid loans Gross and net costs disagree; smaller queues reduce recall Include recoveries, interest, lost lending opportunity and review labor in policy costs; compare capacity, recall and cost jointly on selection data before freezing a proposal Cost sensitivity, missed defaults and queue capacity At 10% volume, LightGBM precision is 37.88% versus 32.38% for the grade rule Use LightGBM as a capacity-limited ranking candidate; retain the grade rule and Logistic as ongoing comparators, and display main contributing factors during review Equal-volume hit rates in later batches, review costs and false flags; the current gain is an offline result These recommendations inform the design of a risk-review pilot. Start with risk segmentation and queue display, record review outcomes, and assess default coverage and costs as loan outcomes mature. Monitor origination vintages so that incomplete outcomes are not mistaken for declining risk. The analysis covers historical approved loans with matured terminal outcomes; the temporal test window contains only 36-month loans. Group associations, fixed-price simulations and a single later window limit transferability. The proposals can guide a pilot; business effects remain to be observed.

This capstone connects model comparison, forecasting and spatial exposure screening to choose methods and sequence further assessment. It covers 1,020 cells in four study boxes, CA, XJ, TK and AU. These labels do not represent entire states or countries. Model–observation comparison starts with physical variables, calendars and sampling, then examines residual error. Cell-level correction lowers population-weighted cell RMSE in all four regions on a common holdout. It does not improve every regional mean or establish the accuracy of site risk rankings. Short-term forecasting requires a choice by region and horizon. Monthly climatology remains the default comparison for CA and XJ; Prophet in TK and 24-month SARIMA in AU merit further validation. Long-term assessment uses differences paired within each climate model. Scenario temperature differences are easier to interpret directly than absolute exceedance counts, which respond to calibration windows and historical frequency bias. Population, built surface and cropland each receive a separate verification list. For 2035–2044 under ssp585, 204 of 268 baseline cell–layer entries meet the proposed priority rule. The next step is to check local uses, population sources and independent temperature data before commissioning finer risk assessment.

Observations are MODIS daytime land surface temperature (LST), February 2000–December 2024; model input is NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 near-surface air temperature (tas). A clear-sky daytime retrieval at an approximately 1 km central pixel differs from the area and daily mean represented by a 0.25° tas cell. Monthly offsets align model means to the LST reference without removing all variable and sampling differences. Product definitions: MODIS and NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 . Spatial totals use the union of the full extracted cells. Population and built surface use 2020 data, and cropland uses 2021 land cover. These population and land distributions stay fixed in future scenarios while temperature changes. GHS and GPW allocate population differently, so similar population-weighted frequencies can accompany different exposure totals. Region Cells GHS people GPW people Total area km² Cropland km² CA 156 1,715,658 1,873,619 95,308.62 3,116.60 XJ 144 44,870 71,823 87,977.18 439.89 TK 144 6,371,851 3,273,523 87,977.18 15,228.79 AU 576 2,372,152 1,953,986 365,561.48 85,052.46 Population and land area are summed over the full study cells. Population is rounded only for display; calculations retain the original decimals. Cropland area is the cropland fraction multiplied by each cell’s spherical area. Each cell uses the 90th percentile (P90) of all its valid monthly temperatures as its threshold. Both observations and future scenarios count only months strictly above that threshold. Exceedance probabilities are estimated separately for each calendar month and then summed across the twelve months. The result, cᵢ, is the cell's annual mean number of exceedance months, measured in months/year. Let wᵢ be the population or relevant land area in cell i. Both indicators below are calculated within each model before summarizing their distribution across models. Weighted annual exceedance frequency describes the average frequency at the locations occupied by people or land. Its unit is months/year: ∑ i w i c i ∑ i w i Total exceedance exposure includes both frequency and exposure size. Population totals use people·months/year, and land totals use m²·months/year: ∑ i w i c i The ratio of population-weighted to area-weighted frequency, and its reciprocal, are calculated within each model before taking the model median. Dividing the two frequency medians in a table would give a different statistic. One cell–calendar-month combination in each of TK and AU has no historical observation. Both observations and models exclude these combinations on the same reference support, while the spatial aggregation remains fixed. Full-year missing-data bounds are assessed separately. The metric describes monthly mean LST exceedances of a local historical threshold, not days in a heatwave.

Ranking tas against LST by raw RMSE mixes mean differences with differences in temporal shape. Report bias first, then centered RMSE (cRMSE), correlation and the standard-deviation ratio. Attach shared time-resampling ranges to historical ranks. The 2,000 resamples draw six whole years with replacement and apply a common missing-data mask after restoring the calendar. These are point-estimate leaders, not proven winners in new years. Even CA spans ranks 1–3, offering no basis for a universal best GCM. Both correction methods use the same 2000–2013 training period, 2014–2024 holdout and observed-month masks. One estimates an offset for each cell; the other applies a regional offset to local tas. Frequency MAE is the absolute error in exceedance probability and is dimensionless. Region Correction method Population-weighted cell RMSE (°C) Population-weighted frequency MAE Regional mean RMSE (°C) CA Cell correction 3.295 0.066 3.246 CA Regional correction applied to local tas 5.787 0.216 3.242 XJ Cell correction 3.176 0.059 2.463 XJ Regional correction applied to local tas 4.313 0.127 2.484 TK Cell correction 3.611 0.049 3.267 TK Regional correction applied to local tas 4.669 0.113 3.281 AU Cell correction 2.860 0.045 2.965 AU Regional correction applied to local tas 4.388 0.109 2.843 Calculation scope: medians across the main 14 models. Lower population-weighted cell error in every region supports using cell correction for further spatial checks. AU regional mean RMSE nevertheless rises from 2.843 to 2.965 °C. Monthly climatology predicts the training-period mean for each calendar month. Seasonal naive repeats the final 12 months of the training series. Lower root mean square error (RMSE) indicates closer agreement with observations. The five test end years are 2016, 2018, 2020, 2022 and 2024, each with a 12- and 24-month window looking backwards. Within each horizon all four methods are scored on identical originally observed months. The two horizons have different forecast origins. Splitting precedes training-only imputation and parameter selection, preventing future observations from influencing training. The table reports the arithmetic mean of five window RMSEs in °C. Scored months sum valid months across the windows; they are not a count of independent observations. Region Horizon (months) Climatology SARIMA Prophet Seasonal naive Scored months CA 12 2.033 2.062 2.211 3.476 57 CA 24 2.636 2.707 2.960 3.394 116 XJ 12 2.238 2.226 2.304 2.273 56 XJ 24 2.028 1.997 2.076 2.466 113 TK 12 2.409 2.441 2.259 3.411 52 TK 24 2.727 2.728 2.604 2.864 104 AU 12 3.077 2.982 2.895 2.788 58 AU 24 2.631 2.522 2.584 3.273 117 SARIMA compares 72 AICc candidates within each training window. Prophet uses yearly seasonality and linear growth. Climatology has lower mean-window RMSE than SARIMA in CA. In XJ, SARIMA reduces this error relative to climatology by about 0.012 °C for 12-month forecasts and 0.031 °C for 24-month forecasts. These small differences do not yet support the more complex method as the default, so both regions retain climatology. Prophet has the lowest mean-window RMSE in TK at both horizons, but wins overall in only 3 of the 5 windows at 12 months and 2 at 24 months. AU's 12-month seasonal naive wins overall in only 1 of the 5 windows. At 24 months, SARIMA wins overall in 2 windows and directly beats climatology in 4. Prophet in TK and 24-month SARIMA in AU therefore remain candidates to test at new forecast origins. Mean-window RMSE averages the RMSE calculated separately in each test window. Pooled RMSE combines squared errors across all scored months, takes their mean, then takes the square root. For AU's 12-month forecasts, this choice changes the relative order of Prophet and SARIMA. Method Mean-window RMSE (°C) Pooled RMSE (°C) Prophet 2.895 3.086 SARIMA 2.982 3.035 Prophet has lower mean-window error, while SARIMA has lower pooled error. The aggregation method therefore needs to be specified before comparing models. MASE uses originally observed 12-month seasonal pairs in training for its denominator. MASE below 1 does not replace a direct test-period comparison with seasonal naive. Five windows establish neither statistical equivalence nor a universal twenty-year minimum for SARIMA. Next, add new test end years at each specified horizon, fixing the scoring mask and aggregation in advance. Track error differences, window wins and residuals before replacing the default baseline.

The near window is 2035–2044 and the far window is 2050–2059. Both assessments use climate-model scenarios without extrapolating a short-term time-series trend. The main ensemble contains 14 models. Calibration windows change some directions. NASA Terra orbit information supports examining observation-time changes alongside clear-sky sampling, regional change and interannual variability. These ranges identify sensitive candidates rather than provide complete future predictive coverage.

Population, built surface and cropland receive separate candidate lists. Within each model, cells are scored by exposure times exceedance frequency, then the median score across models is taken. The quota is one tenth of positive-exposure cells, rounded up. Selection proceeds from the highest score, retaining only positive scores and all ties at the boundary after rounding scores to eight decimal places. Priority candidates must also be retained under all six calibration settings, the 15-model ensemble and every ensemble formed by leaving out one main-ensemble model. Both model selection share and joint time-resampling selection frequency must be at least 80%. Population candidates must additionally survive the switch to GPW. The top-decile and 80% thresholds are proposed scheduling rules for this project. This report compares MODIS land surface temperature with near-surface air temperature from 15 climate models in four study regions during 2015–2020. It examines observation quality, differences between physical variables and bias correction. Error decomposition and day–night comparisons use the 15-model diagnostics; rank uncertainty uses 14 models after excluding a version anomaly. Short-term forecasts are evaluated across five test windows. See the project synthesis for the combined assessment. The 2015–2020 diagnostics with 15 models attribute 74%–97% of regional median RMSE² to mean offset. This supports interpreting variable and sampling differences before cRMSE, correlation and amplitude. Current point-leading rank ranges are CA 1–3, XJ 1–9, TK 1–5 and AU 1–7, offering no universal winner. Retain climatology for short-term comparison and validate regional candidates; aggregate correction improvements do not replace site checks.

What the sponsor asked for. The project addendum of 14 October 2022 states the objective as monitoring and predicting climate-related hazards from the temporal and spatial data in satellite imagery, connecting those to economic data, and informing the risk assessments behind the products S&P sells to its clients. What that placed on the analysis side was to collect and tidy the datasets and to quantify and analyze, per GCM, the difference between observational and derived spatial data in the MODIS and NEX-GDDP NASA databases , with California given as an example region. Two items were listed as business outcomes: collecting and preprocessing publicly available satellite imagery from NASA, and engineering a data pipeline catered toward modeling. Who uses the answer. Putting climate model output onto specific parcels requires three operational answers first: which GCM to feed into a regional heat estimate; whether the scenarios have to be run separately, or one is enough; whether a grid-cell value can stand in for a specific location. Sections 6, 7 and 9 answer these three in turn, each with an uncertainty attached. Scope. The report covers data collection, preprocessing and quantification of differences between observations and models. Long-term scenarios and their use in population and land exposure are described in the scenario and spatial exposure report .

Four regions Code Location Climate NEX 0.25° grid points Valid months (of 72) CA Sierra National Forest, California, USA Montane Mediterranean 156 69 XJ Southern Tarim Basin, Xinjiang, China Hyper-arid desert 144 67 TK Cross-border Iran–Turkmenistan study box Arid continental 144 60 AU Inland New South Wales, Australia Temperate to semi-arid (Southern Hemisphere) 576 72 Sample points are the NEX 0.25° grid-cell centers. Generating them by the rule "grid-cell center inside the bounding box" matches the point counts region by region: CA 156, XJ 144, TK 144, AU 576. That fixes the identity of the sample, and every comparison below sits on the same set of locations. Valid month counts differ by region, and all 12 of TK's missing months fall in the cold season (8 in January to March, 4 in December). Its metrics therefore rest on a warm-season-leaning subset and are not on the same month set as the other three. Cross-region comparisons therefore need to account for the different observed-month sets. MODIS day LST (black) against tas from 15 models (thin lines, ssp585), monthly, 2015–2020. In all four panels the model lines sit wholly below the observations, with a spacing that varies by region. Section 6 takes that spacing apart. Why LST has to be compared with tas The CMIP variable name tas composes t (temperature) with a (air) and s (surface), and the file attributes carry cell_methods: area: time: mean , meaning an average over the cell area and over 24 hours. MODIS LST is point skin temperature at the instant of overpass, around 10:30 for the day pass and 22:30 for the night pass. These are not the same quantity. Within CMIP the variable of the same kind as LST is ts, the model's own skin temperature, but the NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 distribution list carries nine variables and ts is not among them. Observation and model were therefore never the same physical quantity, which is the root of every bias figure in this project and the reason the correction in Section 9 exists. Why this record cannot be differenced against the 2022 extraction The MODIS CSVs in the 2022 deliverables do not hold point values. Across 156 points on a given day, the median count of distinct values is 14 (minimum 0, maximum 18), so roughly eleven points share one number. That extraction used too coarse a scale and returned image-pyramid block means tens of kilometers wide, biasing the record cold by 3.78 °C. Seasonal shape survives intact: the old and new monthly series correlate at r = 0.9902, and their deseasonalized anomalies at r = 0.8394. The two records can therefore corroborate each other in timing but not in level. Subtracting a 2022 bias figure from one in this report measures the extraction settings.

Four method decisions, each with its goal, its alternatives and its cost. 4.1 Splitting RMSE into offset and shape The goal Separate the systematic offset that two different physical quantities must have from the error a model makes in seasonal shape, so that any ranking sits on the second. The choice Two alternatives were on the table. A single RMSE, which is what 2022 used, mixes both terms into one number, so minimizing it amounts to minimizing the offset. Correlation ignores offset entirely, but it also fails to penalize amplitude error. This report uses the identity rmse² = bias² + crmse² and reports all three terms, adding the standard-deviation ratio and Taylor diagrams so that amplitude error stays visible. The procedure Per model, compute bias, cRMSE, correlation, standard-deviation ratio and interannual anomaly correlation, giving a 120-row metric table over four regions and two scenarios. Anomaly correlation is reported for completeness; it measures no skill here, because free-running GCMs are not initialized from observations and are not expected to track individual years. The cost cRMSE is sensitive to the observation cleaning recipe, and how sensitive varies by region (quantified in Section 6.6). Ranking by cRMSE obliges the report to disclose how the observations were aggregated. 4.2 Handling the 360-day calendar with cftime The goal HadGEM3-GC31-MM, KACE-1-0-G and UKESM1-0-LL run on a 360-day calendar, so their time axes cannot be parsed as Gregorian dates. The procedure Files are opened through cftime throughout, and monthly aggregation groups on the first seven characters of the date string, never passing through a Gregorian parse. The cost and the check This step can be tested directly. For one combination (CA, ssp585, HadGEM3-GC31-MM), correct calendar handling gives a monthly RMSE of 8.4599 °C, while treating day N of the 360-day calendar as "2015-01-01 plus N days" gives 9.0725 °C. The value published in 2022 was 9.1046, which differs from the second figure by 0.0321, a gap consistent with a data revision. Only the three 360-day models are affected. A cross-model ranking built on a Gregorian parse is therefore unfair to those three by construction. 4.3 The observation cleaning recipe The goal Cloud contamination makes LST missing on a daily basis. A monthly mean therefore depends on which days and which grid points enter it, and the aggregation rule has to be fixed in advance and published. The choice Two recipes. The 2022-style average replaces the missing marker with NaN, averages however many valid points a day happens to have, then takes the monthly mean. The coverage rule screens by day first, discarding any day with valid points below 50%, then by month, setting a month to NaN if it holds fewer than 10 valid days. The first keeps every month at the price of mixing the cold, low-coverage subsample into the monthly mean; the second pays in missing months for monthly values built on comparable spatial sampling. Results below use the coverage rule, and Section 6.6 reports how the ranks move under the 2022-style average. The procedure The MOD11A1 QC bitmask is applied at extraction. Night series run on a relaxed threshold (at least 10% of points per day, at least 5 valid days per month) because night-time passing rates are much thinner, and night results are used qualitatively only. The cost The coverage rule masks 3 months in CA, 5 in XJ, 12 in TK and none in AU. All 12 of TK's fall in the cold season, leaving every TK metric with that warm-season lean. 4.4 Common time resampling and forecast scoring Historical ranks restore the complete calendar, draw six whole years 2,000 times with common indices for every model, then apply the original shared valid-month mask. Forecast windows are split before training-only imputation and selection. All methods score identical originally observed test months. Rank and forecast results appear in Sections 6.5 and 8.

Observation coverage, seasonal missingness and spatial variation affect the interpretation of model errors and rankings. 5.1 Daytime QC passes half the time; night-time passes an eighth to a third Daytime passing rates are CA 66.40%, TK 59.50%, XJ 56.18% and AU 51.80%; night-time rates are AU 33.65%, TK 31.64%, CA 31.14% and XJ 12.69%. Night coverage is thinner than day coverage by 1.54× in AU up to 4.43× in XJ. Days with no valid observation anywhere in the region (out of 2192) number 136 in AU, 96 in TK, 47 in XJ and 34 in CA. Because the night sample is that thin, night series run on the relaxed threshold and stay qualitative, and Section 9.1 does not subtract one side of the bracket from the other. 5.2 Missingness is strongly seasonal, in the direction climate implies Multi-year extremes of the daytime missing rate by calendar month run from 58% in January to 12% in August for CA, 61% in January to 20% in October for XJ, and 71% in December to 8% in September for TK. AU is the exception, staying between 42% and 54% all year with its peak in July, the Southern Hemisphere winter. Monthly missing-observation rate for CA day and night LST after QC. High in winter, low in summer, with the night curve above the day curve throughout. Missingness here is itself a data product: because it is seasonally structured, no multi-year average over these observations is an equal-weight average, and cold months carry less weight than warm ones. 5.3 The coverage rule costs a different amount in each region Masked months number 3 in CA, 5 in XJ, 12 in TK and 0 in AU, leaving 69, 67, 60 and 72 valid months respectively. Of TK's 12 masked months, 8 fall in January to March and 4 in December, all of them cold-season. The consequence is that every TK metric rests on a warm-season-leaning subset. Wherever a TK number appears alongside another region below, it should be read with that sentence attached. 5.4 The +0.88 °C shift belongs to the aggregation rule; the QC bitmask itself is worth −0.01 °C Moving CA from the 2022-style average to the current recipe raises the monthly regional day LST by 0.88 °C. Almost all of that belongs to the aggregation rule. Holding the QC setting fixed and switching only from the 2022-style average to the coverage rule moves the mean by +0.91 °C, with 2019-11 moving +5.60 °C on its own; holding aggregation fixed and toggling only the QC bitmask moves the mean by −0.01 °C, with no month moving more than 0.24 °C. The mechanism is visible at the level of the raw file: the bitmask removes 877 of 227,933 valid point-days, while the coverage rule discards whole low-coverage days whose surviving pixels are cold. Monthly regional day LST for CA under three processing recipes. Two of the three lines nearly coincide (QC on and off under the same aggregation rule), while the third, the 2022-style average, sits systematically lower. Never quote a bias figure without its cleaning recipe, and note that the decisive part of the recipe is the aggregation rule rather than the QC switch. Subtracting two bias numbers computed under different recipes measures the processing difference. 5.5 The regional mean represents timing well and absolute level poorly Correlation between a single point's series and the regional mean has a median of 0.981 in TK, 0.970 in AU, 0.963 in CA and 0.962 in XJ. Remove the seasonal cycle and those medians fall to 0.865, 0.835, 0.830 and 0.794: most of the original agreement was the annual cycle that every point shares. Per-point long-term means have a standard deviation of 4.20 °C in AU, 4.90 in TK, 8.00 in CA and 8.73 in XJ, and the daily cross-point standard deviation runs XJ 8.6, CA 8.3, TK 5.4, AU 4.6 °C. Per-point dispersion in CA: cross-point standard deviation of daily day LST at left (30-day rolling mean), the regional mean against the per-point range in the middle, and the distribution of per-point correlations with the regional mean at right. Since each model supplies exactly one regional-mean tas, this dispersion is also the dispersion of the per-point bias behind every bias figure in this report. A 0.25° cell is not a station value , and using it as one means accepting a 4.2 to 8.7 °C spread of per-point means. 5.6 Diurnal range sorts with aridity Mean day-minus-night LST is 31.8 °C in XJ, 22.9 in TK, 18.7 in CA and 16.2 in AU. For CA the monthly climatology of that range runs from 23.5 °C in May down to 11.3 °C in January. This quantity sets the scale of the day-side bias: the same model tas necessarily sits further from day LST where the diurnal range is larger. All four numbers should be read as upper bounds, because the day and night series come from different QC subsamples and surviving night pixels favor clear nights.

Median day-side bias is −19.0 °C in XJ, −15.8 in TK, −12.4 in CA and −10.8 in AU; median night-side bias is +12.7, +6.8, +6.6 and +5.3 °C. CA: MODIS day LST (solid black), night LST (dashed gray) and tas from 15 models (thin red, ssp585). Model lines run as a bundle between the two observed series. This sign relation confirms that the offset is a difference of physical quantities rather than model error, but it does not discriminate between models . Since tas is a 24-hour mean and day LST is skin temperature around noon, the relation is close to inevitable for any reasonable temperature series. 6.2 Offset accounts for 74% to 97% of squared error Regional medians of bias² as a share of RMSE² are AU 74%, CA 79%, TK 90% and XJ 97%, and across all 60 region-model combinations the share spans 0.48 to 0.97. Share of RMSE² carried by bias², per model, in CA, with a regional median of 79%. This is the quantitative form of "choosing by RMSE is choosing by offset": offset takes 79% of the squared error in CA, and 97% in XJ, which leaves 3% there for models to compete over. 6.3 The choice of variable matters more than the choice of model Cross-model spread within a month (largest minus smallest of the 15 values) averages 8.7 °C in CA, 8.0 in TK, 7.3 in AU and 7.1 in XJ, all smaller than the width of the day-night envelope. 7.1 RMSE and cRMSE sort the four regions in nearly opposite orders Median RMSE runs AU 12.61 < CA 14.01 < TK 16.63 < XJ 19.32 °C. By cRMSE the order almost reverses: XJ 3.55 < TK 5.24 < AU 6.33 < CA 6.44 °C. Correlation follows cRMSE, highest in XJ at 0.98, then TK 0.96, AU 0.94 and CA 0.92. Metric distributions by region (ssp585, 15 models). By RMSE, XJ is the worst region; by cRMSE and correlation it is the best. One mechanism drives both: an arid surface runs much hotter than the air above it, which inflates the offset term. Aridity also means clear skies, which makes the seasonal cycle cleanest and pushes cRMSE down. This resolves what the 2022 record reported without explaining, namely one region showing high RMSE together with a high R². Both statements describe different terms of the same identity, each correct on its own, and they look contradictory only when treated as one number. 7.2 Historical point estimates and current rank ranges The original 15-model figures describe regional error patterns. Current main-14 point leaders and rank ranges are given in §6.5; their order does not establish significant superiority. 7.3 Bias and cRMSE are two independent axes Pooling all 60 region-model points, bias and cRMSE correlate at +0.88; within regions the correlation is −0.20 in CA, +0.39 in XJ, +0.56 in TK and −0.60 in AU. Pooled agreement comes from the aridity gradient entering both terms at once, so it describes a regional contrast and not a model-level relationship. Bias on the horizontal axis, cRMSE on the vertical, colored by region. Four clusters separate horizontally (the regional effect) and each cluster is narrow vertically (the model effect). Knowing that a model has the smallest offset in a region says almost nothing about whether its shape is the best there. Shape can only be read off cRMSE, and cRMSE has to be read with the intervals from Section 6.5. On the Taylor diagrams each region forms its own cluster. Standard-deviation ratios are below 1 throughout, because the annual amplitude of daily mean air temperature is smaller than that of midday skin temperature. Pairing these two variables produces that gap; no model defect is involved. Cross-model range in correlation is 0.012 in XJ, 0.036 in TK, 0.044 in CA and 0.059 in AU, while the range in standard-deviation ratio is 0.121 in TK, 0.091 in CA, 0.086 in AU and 0.070 in XJ. Which region is "most dispersed" depends on which axis is read. 7.4 Historical scenario comparison and long-term use Small historical scenario differences in 2015–2020 establish neither statistical equivalence nor interchangeability in future periods. Long-term reporting pairs ssp585−ssp126 within each model and retains both scenarios and their difference distribution; see the synthesis .

Sections 6 and 7 point the same way: estimating the offset well is worth more than choosing among 15 models. This section tests whether that route works. 9.1 What the recipe rests on Model tas falls between night and day LST in 15 of 15 cases in all four regions, running 10.8 to 19.0 °C below day LST and 5.3 to 12.7 °C above night LST as regional medians (Section 6.1). Because the sign and magnitude of that offset follow from a physical relation and vary systematically by region, the offset is estimable. Ensemble-median bias by region: negative against day LST everywhere, positive against night LST everywhere, with the day-side gap widening with aridity. This structure is what the correction rests on , since the quantity to estimate is not which model is right but how much to add going from tas to day LST. Two limits apply: the bracket does not discriminate between models, and the two columns rest on different month sets, so they cannot be subtracted. 9.2 Holdout test: raw tas, then one constant, then twelve monthly values Offsets are fitted on 2015–2018 and tested on 2019–2020. The valid-month counts are: Region Calibration months Test months CA 46 23 XJ 44 23 TK 40 20 AU 48 24 Median RMSE against daytime LST is: Form of correction CA XJ TK AU Raw tas, uncorrected 13.37 19.17 15.89 12.29 One regional constant 6.74 3.67 4.62 6.54 Twelve monthly values 3.78 2.36 3.63 2.51 Reference: climatology of the observations 3.08 1.85 2.80 2.05 Units are °C. Cells in the first three rows are medians over the 15 models; the last row involves no model at all. No intervals are attached: the test window is the two years 2019–2020, every cell comes from that single window, and Section 9.4 carries the limit into the usage constraints. The monthly form beats the single constant in all four regions by 1.0 to 4.0 °C. One regional constant already takes the apparent error from 12–19 °C down to the 3.7–6.7 °C range, which is where the return on correcting exceeds the return on model selection. 9.3 Climatology and free-running models Observed monthly climatology has lower error in the original holdout. Free-running GCMs are not synchronized with actual year-specific weather, so monthly errors include differences between unaligned realizations. This is not a theorem that beating climatology is impossible. Compare distributions and pathway differences for future scenarios, and test short-term methods directly with rolling windows. 9.4 Local reference and scope Monthly offsets require local observations. Findings do not directly transfer to locations without a usable satellite record; cross-location transfer needs separate validation. Current spatial common-holdout checks and candidate stability are in synthesis §3 and §8. Mean correction does not ensure accurate tail frequency.

This capstone connects model comparison, forecasting and spatial exposure screening to choose methods and sequence further assessment. It covers 1,020 cells in four study boxes, CA, XJ, TK and AU. These labels do not represent entire states or countries. Model–observation comparison starts with physical variables, calendars and sampling, then examines residual error. Cell-level correction lowers population-weighted cell RMSE in all four regions on a common holdout. It does not improve every regional mean or establish the accuracy of site risk rankings. Short-term forecasting requires a choice by region and horizon. Monthly climatology remains the default comparison for CA and XJ; Prophet in TK and 24-month SARIMA in AU merit further validation. Long-term assessment uses differences paired within each climate model. Scenario temperature differences are easier to interpret directly than absolute exceedance counts, which respond to calibration windows and historical frequency bias. Population, built surface and cropland each receive a separate verification list. For 2035–2044 under ssp585, 204 of 268 baseline cell–layer entries meet the proposed priority rule. The next step is to check local uses, population sources and independent temperature data before commissioning finer risk assessment.

The observation-quality, night-sample and central-pixel diagnostics cover 2015–2020. All four regions are selected study boxes, so their metrics do not directly represent entire states or countries. Night-time data use looser coverage rules, and day–night differences also reflect sampling. The synthesis presents cell-level correction and longer-record results; site applications still require independent observations.

This report uses observation and model records spanning 2000–2024 to compare short-term forecasting methods, examine observed trends and assess bias-correction stability. Forecasts use five test windows and two horizons, with imputation and parameter selection confined to training. Calibration is assessed on a common recent holdout and under alternative windows and model ensembles. Short-term forecasting requires a choice by region and horizon. Monthly climatology remains the default comparison for CA and XJ; Prophet in TK and 24-month SARIMA in AU merit further validation. Long-term assessment uses differences paired within each climate model. Scenario temperature differences are easier to interpret directly than absolute exceedance counts, which respond to calibration windows and historical frequency bias.

A longer record permits comparisons across forecast windows, tests of trend endpoint sensitivity and checks of correction stability. Record length alone does not establish model suitability, and residual diagnostics cannot define a universal twenty-year minimum. Cell-level validation and exposure screening are presented in the scenario and spatial exposure report .

3.1 Observations: 299 months per region MODIS daytime land surface temperature now covers 2000-02 to 2024-12 in all four regions, 299 months each. The coverage rule (at least 50% of grid points per day, at least 10 valid days per month) costs a different amount in each: Region Valid months Masked Masked share CA 286 13 4.3% XJ 278 21 7.0% TK 245 54 18.1% AU 292 7 2.3% TK loses close to one month in five, and the losses concentrate in the cold season: 50 of its 54 masked months fall between December and March. That warm-season lean follows every TK figure in this report. Monthly daytime land surface temperature in the four regions, with red rules marking months the coverage rule removes. The TK panel carries several times the density of the other three, and its losses arrive in clusters every winter. Any seasonal quantity for TK therefore needs its own caveat. 3.2 Consistency in the overlapping period The six-year and long-record extractions both cover 2015–2020. Pairing originally observed months gives 69, 67, 60 and 72 months in CA, XJ, TK and AU. The maximum absolute difference is 0.0000 °C, correlation is 1.000000, and masked-month counts agree in every region. This supports consistent data definitions in the overlapping period. 3.3 Model series: historical joined to SSP NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 distributes each model's SSP run from 2015 onward. Before that comes the historical run, which in CMIP6 is the simulation the SSP run continues from. Joining the two at 2014–2015 makes the model series as long as the observations. Two checks establish that the join is legitimate. All fifteen models carry the same ensemble-member label and the same file version on both sides, and every spliced series is 300 months long in every region. The seam itself is measured as the difference between the five-year climatologies of the same calendar month on either side. The other fourteen models sit at +0.28 ± 0.18 °C, a range of −0.15 to +0.50; CMCC-CM2-SR5 sits at −0.13 °C, 2.2 standard deviations away. Annual means by region: model tas as thin lines, observations in blue, the 2014–2015 seam dashed. The model lines run continuously through the seam with no step. The black line is CMCC-CM2-SR5, which sits above the rest of the field throughout without jumping at the join, and §8 explains why.

Four decisions, each with its purpose, the alternatives, and what it costs. 4.1 The splice The goal Give the model series a window as long as the observations. The choice The alternative is to use the SSP segment alone and confine the analysis to 2015 onward, which leaves a window of six to ten years. Joining the historical segment is legitimate only if both segments are the same simulation, so the ensemble-member label and the file version are checked model by model, and all fifteen agree. The cost The scenario branch begins only in 2015, so 2000–2014 is one line shared by all scenarios. Every long-window result in this report is therefore scenario-agnostic, and any comparison between scenarios still has to be made after 2015. 4.2 Missingness by use Historical trend diagnostics compare original NaNs, interpolation and complete calendar months. Forecasting splits the test window before training-only filling and excludes originally missing test months from scoring. Correction and frequency comparisons retain original masks and the full calendar; dropping missing rows must not turn nonadjacent months into neighbors. 4.3 Forecast windows and aggregation Monthly climatology predicts the training-period mean for each calendar month. Seasonal naive repeats the final 12 months of the training series. Lower root mean square error (RMSE) indicates closer agreement with observations. The five test end years are 2016, 2018, 2020, 2022 and 2024, each with a 12- and 24-month window looking backwards. Within each horizon all four methods are scored on identical originally observed months. The two horizons have different forecast origins. Splitting precedes training-only imputation and parameter selection, preventing future observations from influencing training. Full results and the two RMSE aggregations appear in §5. 4.4 Calibration and test split for the correction The goal Measure how the correction behaves outside the window it was fitted on, over a span long enough to distinguish it from a climatology. The procedure Twelve monthly offsets are fitted on 2000–2013 and tested from 2014 onward, scoring 113 to 129 months per region. The same offsets are then fitted separately on two decades and compared directly in level and in shape. The cost The calibration period falls entirely inside the historical segment while the test period is mostly the SSP segment. This split tests whether offsets fitted in the historical segment transfer to the scenario segment.

This report compares two climate scenarios for 2035–2044 and 2050–2059, examining temperature differences, exceedance frequency and sensitivity to calibration and model choice. Calculations are completed within each model before summarizing model distributions, providing the temperature basis for population and land-exposure screening. The near window is 2035–2044 and the far window is 2050–2059. Both assessments use climate-model scenarios without extrapolating a short-term time-series trend. The main ensemble contains 14 models. CMCC-CM2-SR5 is available only as unrevised v1.0 data and has a version-related temperature-offset anomaly. Its influence is tested separately in a sensitivity analysis including all 15 models.

This report combines cell-level temperature with population, built surface and cropland to identify locations for priority checks. Contributions and list stability are calculated separately for the three exposure layers, while a common holdout evaluates correction error. The resulting lists guide the collection of resident, asset and agricultural data.
Temperature differences compare pathways; absolute exceedance frequency informs conditional follow-up checks. Pairing and counting are performed within each model.
